client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. I know this week was a rough one — before we get into anything, I just want to check in. How are you feeling right now, sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Irritated. My mom basically wouldn't let up until I agreed to come back, so... here I am. I don't really know what I'm supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because of pressure from your mom, and that doesn't sit well with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — I love her, but she acts like I'm some kind of alcoholic because I have a glass of wine at night. I had a hard week, okay? It got a little out of hand but that doesn't mean there's a... like, a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about that — when you say it got out of hand, what did that actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay, fine. I had more than one glass. A few nights in a row. And Marcus — my husband — he saw, and he got this look on his face, like he was scared or something, and then he called my mom. And now everyone's treating me like I'm... I don't know. Like I'm some kind of mess. It's humiliating.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds really painful — to feel like the people who love you are looking at you differently, when you're already running on empty.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. It is. I'm just so tired. Like, all the time. Ellie doesn't sleep more than two hours at a stretch, Marcus is back at work, and I'm just — I'm doing it all, you know? The wine just... it takes the edge off. It's the only thing that feels like mine at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The one thing that feels like it belongs to you. I hear that. What are you hoping it gives you that nothing else does right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Quiet, I guess. Like my brain just shuts up for a little while. I'm not — I'm not trying to be a bad mom. I always wait until she's down. I'm not holding her or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're working hard to keep those things separate — the drinking and being there for Ellie.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I am. I mean... I try to. But last Tuesday, she woke up around 2am and I had had — more than I realized. And I was just so out of it, I couldn't get to her fast enough. She was screaming and Marcus had to get up. And I just stood in the doorway feeling like...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What were you feeling in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Awful. Like... the worst I've felt since she was born. I kept thinking — what if something had actually been wrong? What if she needed me and I was... like that. I can't. I don't want to be that mom.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that that moment scared you — that says something real about who you are. You care deeply about being there for her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do. She's everything. I just... I didn't expect it to be this hard. I pictured it differently. I thought I'd be better at it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I've got this — you're exhausted, you're carrying most of this on your own right now, and the wine has been your way of getting a break from all of it. But Tuesday night something shifted. You saw what it could cost, and that shook you. And underneath everything, being present for Ellie — that matters more to you than anything else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I don't want to keep doing this. I just — I don't know what else to do when I hit that wall at night and there's nothing left.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's actually a really important place to be — knowing you want something different, even if the how is still fuzzy. What do you think one small thing might look like, just to start?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... maybe I call my mom instead of just pouring a glass. She keeps offering to come over in the evenings and I keep telling her no. Maybe I should just... let her.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know this probably wasn't how you were planning to spend your afternoon. Before we get into anything, I just want to hear from you directly — what's your understanding of why you're here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my friend basically forced me to come. And honestly I don't even see the point because I didn't do anything wrong. Like, literally everyone at my school drinks. Everyone. So I don't get why I'm the one sitting in some office having to explain myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels really unfair — like you were singled out for something everyone else does without any consequences.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. There were like thirty other kids at that event and somehow I'm the one who ends up here. It's — it's such a joke. I'm not some alcoholic. I'm not like... I'm a normal teenager doing normal teenager things and now everyone's acting like I committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like when you got pulled aside — in that moment, what was going through your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Humiliating. Like completely humiliating. And then my parents found out and they're acting like I'm some kind of — ugh. It's just drinking. It's not like I robbed a bank. I don't understand why everybody's making this into some huge thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds genuinely rough — the embarrassment, your parents' reaction, now being here. And I notice you're someone who clearly cares about how she's seen. You're not okay with just being labeled.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right, because I'm not a bad person. I'm not trying to be some — some problem kid. I just went to a party. That's it. I shouldn't have to sit here and defend that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And I'm not here to put you on trial. I'm genuinely curious about something though — how do you see your drinking compared to other people your age? Like, in your own mind, where do you fall?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't drink every day. It's mostly just parties, like weekends. I'm not some — I know what actually messed up looks like and that's not me. I'm still going to school, my grades are fine, I'm not like... I don't need it or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So for you it's social — tied to situations, not something you're reaching for on your own. And that distinction feels important to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Because it is different. I know kids who are actually... like, actually struggling with it. And I see what that does to them and I'm like, that's not me. I still have my stuff together. So yeah, it matters.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've clearly thought about where your line is. What would it look like for you if drinking did start to become a problem — like, what would that even look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I guess if it started messing with stuff. Like school, or if I was like... hiding it all the time or something. But that's not happening. So... I don't know. Right now it's fine. It's just fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing, because I think there's something real here. You feel unfairly singled out — and that anger makes sense. You also have a pretty clear internal map of what 'too far' would look like: hiding it, grades slipping, needing it. You're watching for those things. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I haven't really said it out loud like that but... yeah. I don't want it to turn into something. It's not supposed to be a thing, it's just — it's supposed to be fun. That's all it's supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want it to become something it isn't right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And like... okay, my friend — the one who made me come here — she said she got scared one night. About me. And I kind of brushed her off when she brought it up but... I don't know. I keep thinking about that. Like why was she scared? That kind of... stuck.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like part of you actually heard her, even if it was hard to show it in the moment. What do you think she saw that night that scared her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I'm not totally sure. I think maybe I just — I went further than usual that night. I don't remember all of it, honestly, which is... I mean. That's probably not great, right? Like, I know that's not great.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in. I'm Marcus. Before we get into anything — you showing up today, after the week it sounds like you've had, that took something. So tell me, what's your sense of why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor sent me. Said I need to talk to someone about my drinking. Honestly? I think he's way outta line. I've been doing construction for twenty years, I drink a few beers after work — that's just what you do. I'm not some kind of alcoholic sitting in a gutter somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're sitting, this whole thing feels like a massive overreaction. You drink after work, your doctor decides that's a problem, and now you're here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. You work ten hours in the heat pouring concrete, your back's killing you, you come home and crack open a beer — that's not a disease, that's just... that's Tuesday. My guys would lose it if they knew I was sitting here right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned the ER. Walk me through what happened there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That was nothing. I had some pain in my side, my wife freaked out and called 911 — I didn't even want to go. They did a bunch of tests and suddenly everybody's got an opinion on how I run my life. I'm fine. I walked outta there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't want to go, it felt unnecessary, and now it's like everyone jumped on this thing at once — doctor, wife, now me.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ganging up on me — yeah, that's the word. I've seen counselors before, you know. Twice. Didn't do a damn thing. No offense. So I don't really know why this time is supposed to be different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm not here to sell you on anything. But the blood tests the ER ran — what did they actually tell you about what those showed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They said my liver enzymes were elevated. But look — that can come from a ton of things. I've been taking ibuprofen for my back for like six months straight. That messes with your liver too, right? That's probably what it is. My doctor just... the second I told him how many beers I drink, that was it for him. Case closed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you is really holding onto that. Hoping it's the ibuprofen.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...It could be. Nobody's proven it's not. The ER doc, my regular doc — neither one of 'em said for certain it was the drinking. They assumed. That's all. I've been drinking a six-pack a night for fifteen years and I haven't dropped dead yet, have I.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just lay out what I'm hearing, make sure I've got it right. You've been drinking after work for years — it's how you unwind, it's part of the culture you work in. Then you end up in the ER with pain in your side, the bloodwork comes back flagged, and now your doctor, your wife, and I are all coming at you about it. And your position is: everyone's jumping to conclusions off one data point. That about cover it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's — yeah, that's it. I mean... look, I'm not saying the numbers were perfect. But one test. It's a lot of noise all at once and I just — I don't know. I'm not ready to blow up my whole routine because everybody panicked.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in anyway. A lot of guys in your spot wouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife basically dragged me. I'm not gonna pretend I was jumping at the chance to be here. But she... she doesn't scare easy, you know? She's been with me through some rough stuff. She was scared. Like, actually scared. That's not — she's not like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like, seeing her that scared?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I didn't like it. I really didn't. She's not — she's not dramatic. So when she's that shaken up, that means something. I haven't really let myself think about it that way until just now, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got someone who knows you better than almost anybody, who doesn't rattle, who was scared enough to call 911 — and even if you're not ready to call the drinking a problem, something about that landed. That's worth paying attention to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I'm not — I'm not agreeing to anything here. But... I don't know. Maybe I can at least hear what you have to say. I'm here, right?

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you back. Last time we ended on a pretty good note — you'd had a couple solid weeks. What's been going on since then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's been a mess. Sarah got a lawyer — a real shark — and now she's trying to limit my time with the kids. So yeah, if I've been drinking more, can you blame me? Like, what am I supposed to do, just sit there and take it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like you're being pushed out of your own family. That's a gut punch.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It IS a gut punch. Twenty-two years. Twenty-two years and she just — I don't know, rewrites the whole story like I was the problem the entire time. And now I'm the bad guy because I have a few drinks to get through the night. That's just... it's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking — what's it actually doing for you when you get home at night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... quiets things down. In my head. Otherwise I'm just lying there running through every argument, every — I don't know. It's like a hamster wheel. I can't make it stop on my own.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So right now it's the only off switch you've got.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Pretty much. I mean — I know you're going to say it's not a great coping mechanism or whatever, but... the apartment's empty. The kids are at her place. It's just me and four walls. What else am I supposed to do with that?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not here to lecture you about coping skills. But I want to be straight with you — three weeks ago you sat in that chair and told me you were starting to feel like yourself again. What happened to that guy?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That guy thought things were stabilizing. Then the lawyer stuff hit and it just... pulled the rug out. I guess I thought the worst was behind me. Turns out it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You'd built something real over those weeks, and then something knocked it down. That's genuinely hard. When you think about where the drinking has taken you the last couple weeks — what worries you most?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The kids. If I show up to a custody hearing and they've got... documentation, or some witness saying whatever — I could lose even more time with them. And that is the one thing I... I won't let that happen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your kids are the line you won't cross.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, they are. And the thing is — I know when I'm like this, I'm not... I'm not who they need. Jake called me last Tuesday and I could hear it in my own voice. Like I could tell. And he got quieter. My sixteen-year-old went quiet because of me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You noticed it in the moment. And you're still sitting with it now — you didn't just bury it. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I cried after we hung up. Which is — I don't do that. I didn't used to. I don't know what I am anymore, honestly. But I don't want to become someone my kids have to manage. Like some fragile thing they have to be careful around. That's not — that's not their job.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull this together, because I think you just said something important. You came in angry — rightfully so — about the legal situation. But underneath that, what I'm hearing is fear. Fear of losing your kids. And you already know the drinking is putting exactly that at risk. You had three good weeks. That's not luck — that's you. So let me ask: what was working then that you've stopped doing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was going to the gym. Even just three mornings a week. It gave me somewhere to be, something to do with the... the energy, I guess. I'd be tired in a good way and actually sleep. I just stopped when all the legal stuff started piling up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The gym gave you structure, a reason to get up, and it worked. That's not gone — that's still there waiting for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. I think I've been waiting to feel ready and that's... that's never coming, is it. I'd rather Jake see me fighting for myself than just — just going under. That's not the dad I want to be.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you came in today. It takes something to walk through that door, especially for the first time. So... what would you like me to understand about what's been going on for you lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... honestly I'm not totally sure what I'm supposed to say here. My wife — Sarah — she basically said she needed to see me do something, like actually try to fix things, or she didn't know if we could keep going. So. Here I am. I do want things to be better. I want us to be better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because Sarah matters to you — a lot — and you don't want to lose her. And part of you genuinely wants things to be different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's right. I mean, I love her. And I know things have been... not great. I've been kind of checked out. I can feel it but I just — I don't know how to stop the spiral, you know? Like every time I try to focus on the dissertation, I hit this wall and then... I don't know. A drink kind of takes the edge off. And then another one. It's not like I'm some — it's not like I think I have a drinking problem. I just... I don't know what else to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That wall you keep hitting... what does that actually feel like, when you're sitting there with your work and it just won't come?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like — okay, so I'm a fifth-year PhD student. Computational neuroscience. And everyone around me just seems to get it. Like they're writing papers, presenting at conferences, and I'm sitting there reading the same paragraph for the fourth time and nothing is going in. My advisor pulled me aside last month and said my last chapter draft was 'unfocused.' That word just keeps playing in my head. Unfocused. And I'm thinking, what if he's right? What if I'm just not actually smart enough to be here?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word landed hard. Unfocused. And somewhere underneath it, there's a fear that it might actually be true — that maybe you don't really belong there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. God, I hate saying that out loud. I've never actually said that to anyone. But like, I grew up in a small town in Ohio, nobody in my family went to college, and now I'm supposed to be getting a PhD at a research university and giving talks and — it's like I'm waiting for someone to figure out I faked my way in. Which is stupid. I know it's stupid. But when I drink, at least that voice kind of... quiets down. For a little while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying that alone for a long time. And you found something that gives you a break from it, even if just for a few hours. That makes a lot of sense. And yet — you're here. Which tells me something about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know what it tells you. Honestly. I feel like I'm just — I'm failing at everything right now. My research is behind, my advisor is losing patience, and Sarah — she cried last week, like really cried, and I just sat there like an idiot. I didn't know what to say. I still don't. I'm supposed to be someone who figures things out. That's literally my job. And I can't figure out my own life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text:
...

Sarah crying. And you sitting there, not knowing how to reach her. That sounds really lonely. For both of you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It is. It really is. I think that's the part that — like, the dissertation I can maybe fix eventually. But if I lose her... I don't know who I am without her. She's been with me through all of this. Every rejection letter, every failed experiment, every time I wanted to quit. She was the one who said keep going. And now I'm the reason she's crying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's been your person through all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. She is. And I've been... I don't even know when it started. Like really started. It was maybe a drink or two on a Friday after a bad week and now it's — most nights. Sometimes I don't even realize how much until I'm trying to do something the next morning and I can't think straight. And Sarah notices. She doesn't say anything anymore. She just gets this look. And that look is worse than anything she could actually say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine finishing your PhD — actually defending, walking out of that room with a doctorate — is Sarah there, in that picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yes. She's — that's the first thing I see. Her face. I've thought about that moment so many times. It's like the thing that keeps me going when nothing else does. She'd be so proud. I'd be so proud. And I... huh. I hadn't thought about it like that. Like, if I keep going the way I am, that moment might not exist. Either because I don't finish, or because she's not there anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I've heard from you today, because I think you've said some really important things. You came here because you love Sarah and you don't want to lose her. You've been fighting this feeling for years that you don't belong — carrying it alone, quietly. You found that drinking turns that voice down for a while. And somewhere along the way it became most nights. And when you imagine the finish line — defending your dissertation — Sarah's face is the first thing you see. It sounds like you already know what matters most to you. You haven't lost sight of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it all together like that... yeah. Yeah, I do know. I've just been so in my head that I couldn't — I mean, I still don't know what to actually do. But I think I want to try. Like actually try, not just show up here so Sarah thinks I'm trying. I want to figure this out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That shift — from 'I'm here because Sarah needs to see me try' to 'I want to figure this out for myself' — that's not nothing. That's actually everything. So I want to ask you: what feels like one small thing, just one, that you could do differently this week? Not to fix it all. Just one thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I don't know, maybe I could tell Sarah about the imposter syndrome stuff. The Ohio thing. I've never actually told her why I drink, like the real reason. I've just let her think I'm stressed about deadlines. She deserves to know the actual thing. And maybe — maybe that's a start.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know you were referred by Dr. Patel, and sometimes showing up to a place like this isn't exactly how people picture their Tuesday going. I just want to start by hearing what's been going on for you lately — in your own words, no agenda.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... he said I should come so. Here I am. I've been a nurse for eight years, ER, and the last few have just been... a lot. I don't really know what I'm supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eight years in the ER — and the last few have felt especially heavy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's one way to put it. Look, I know why I'm here. Something came up in my bloodwork or whatever. And yeah, I drink more than I used to. But after a twelve-hour shift watching people die, a glass of wine is the only thing that actually quiets everything down. So I don't really see it as, like, a problem problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does 'quieting everything down' actually look like — what is it quieting?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just... the noise. The replaying. I'll get home at 2 AM and my brain's still running a code — I'm still hearing the monitors, the family crying in the hallway. I can't just turn it off. And I've tried, okay? The meditation apps, the hot showers, talking to people. Nothing sticks. The wine becomes two, then three, and I know that's not great, but... nothing else works. And I've already done the counseling thing twice and it didn't help, so honestly I don't know what we're supposed to do here that's different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's not that you haven't tried to cope differently — you've actually put in real effort. The drinking just happens to be the one thing that gives you some actual relief from what sounds like a pretty relentless loop in your head. And two counselors who didn't help... I'd be skeptical too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. They kept doing breathing exercises and telling me to journal. I'm like... do you know what I saw last Tuesday? Journaling isn't going to touch that. I don't know. Maybe nothing is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying an enormous amount, and you've been doing it mostly alone — holding it together for your patients, your team, everyone. And then you get home and there's nothing left, so you reach for the one thing that gives you a few hours of quiet. That's not weakness. That's someone who ran out of other options.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It's just exhausting. Being the one who holds it together for everyone and then coming home to an empty apartment and just... there's nothing left to hold. The wine fills something. Even if it's just for a few hours.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Outside of work — what does life look like right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I've kind of stopped doing things I used to like. I used to run — like, half marathons, I loved it. Haven't laced up in over a year. My friends have basically stopped inviting me out because I either cancel or I show up and I'm not really there. And my sister called last month and said she was worried about me, and I just got so defensive, we didn't talk for two weeks. That was... that was hard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been pulling away — from running, from your friends, from your sister. And it sounds like when she reached out, part of you felt the weight of that, even if the defensive reaction came first.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And the thing that actually scares me... it's work. Last month I almost made a medication error. I caught it in time, nothing happened, but — I have never done that. Eight years, my hands just know what to do. But that day I was exhausted and I'd had way too much the night before and I just... I can't be that person. I can't be the nurse who hurts someone because she can't get herself together.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back, because I think it matters. You walked in here skeptical — you've done this before, it didn't work, you're tired of being told to breathe. And underneath all of that, there's someone who's still showing up to one of the hardest jobs there is, who still cares deeply about not hurting anyone, whose instincts are sharp enough that she caught that error. And now you're telling me the drinking is starting to touch the one thing you've always been able to count on — your clinical judgment. That feels like a different kind of line.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. I've told myself for months it's fine, it's manageable, I'm just decompressing like anyone would. But... yeah. Hearing it like that. It's not fine. I don't want to be fine with it anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So what would 'not being fine with it anymore' actually look like — what would changing something feel like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Like... I want to be able to come home from a hard shift and eventually sleep without needing something to get there. I want to run again. I want to call my sister and not have to pretend everything's okay. I don't know if I want to never drink again — I honestly don't know about that part yet. But I don't want it to be the only thing that works. That's the part that has to change.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's an honest answer — and a real one. What would it mean to you to get to a place where it's not the only thing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... I don't know, like I'm actually taking care of myself instead of just surviving shifts. Being someone my sister doesn't have to worry about. Being the nurse I actually want to be — not the one running on fumes and wine. I don't know if I'm there yet. But I think I want to try. Actually try. Not just because Dr. Patel told me to.

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. That means something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... I almost didn't. I was going to cancel like three times this morning, I even had the message typed out. I don't really know why I came.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something made you put the phone down and come anyway. What was that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My friend — the one who kind of pushed me to do this in the first place — she texted me this morning. Just checking in, nothing pushy. And I just... I don't know, I didn't want to have to tell her I bailed. Or maybe I didn't want to tell myself I did.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to ask you straight — how did the week go with the drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... about the same, honestly. I told myself I'd try to skip at least one night and I didn't. But it's not like I'm getting, like, drunk — it's just a glass or two after Mia goes down. It's the only time the house is actually quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's become the signal that the day is finally yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like... that's the only thing that feels like mine right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What happens when you imagine giving that up — even just for one night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's terrifying. I know that sounds dramatic but... I don't have anything else right now. I'm not sleeping well, I feel like I don't even know who I am anymore. I used to have a whole life and now it's just feeding schedules and crying, and I love her, I really do, but it's — it's a lot. The wine is the one thing I look forward to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What you're describing — the lost identity, the exhaustion, needing something just for you — that's incredibly common in new mothers, and it makes complete sense that you landed on alcohol, because it works. In the short term. The question worth sitting with is what it's costing you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My partner — he said something kind of similar. He's not angry, he's been really supportive actually, but he mentioned that I seem more on edge the next day. And I've noticed it too. Like, I sleep but I don't feel rested. I wake up kind of... already behind somehow.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've talked a lot about what you need right now. I want to ask about Mia — when you picture her growing up, what kind of mom do you want her to see?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Um... I want to be present. Like actually there, not just in the room. My mom was kind of... checked out a lot when I was little. She wasn't a bad person, she was dealing with her own stuff, but I always felt like I had to compete for her attention. And I swore — I mean I swore I would never... yeah. I don't want Mia to feel that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a small thing you just said. You have a really clear sense of who you want to be for her — and I hear underneath that some real fear that the drinking might be pulling you away from it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think it is. I haven't let myself say that out loud until just now, but... yeah. Some mornings I'm foggy and short with everyone and she's just a baby, she doesn't deserve that. She's not doing anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've been hearing today. You came in even when part of you wanted to walk away — that took something. You've noticed the drinking isn't actually giving you the rest you're looking for. Your partner sees a change in you the next day. And underneath all of it there's this clear, strong value: you want Mia to have what you didn't. You want to actually be there for her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. All of that is true. I think I've known it, I just kept kind of... talking myself around it. Telling myself it wasn't that big a deal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you just named — where do you want to go from here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I want to actually try. Like, really try this time, not just say I will. I don't know exactly what that looks like yet but... I don't want to keep doing this and then look up in five years and realize I was there but I wasn't really there. That scares me more than stopping.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know this isn't always an easy decision. Before we get into anything, I just want to ask — what would make today feel worth your time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't know why I'm here. My girlfriend basically said — look, you go or I'm done. So. Here I am. I don't think I have some kind of... problem. I've been going through a lot. Anyone would drink more.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you showed up because someone you care about asked you to. That's not nothing — even if it doesn't feel like your idea.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I'm not gonna pretend I wanted to sit on a couch and talk about my feelings. That's not — I'm not that guy. And look, my ex-wife is the one who blew everything up. She decided she was done. I didn't choose any of this. So yeah, I come home to an empty apartment and I have a drink. That's not alcoholism, that's Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four months ago your whole life looked completely different. Walk me through what that's actually been like — not the legal stuff, just... what it's been like to live it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... I don't know. I mean, I lost the house. I only see my kids every other weekend. I'm living in this apartment — smells like dog, walls are thin, I can hear my neighbor watching TV at midnight. I went from... I had a life, you know? And now I come home and there's just nothing there. So yeah, I pour a scotch. Maybe two. It helps me get to sleep. That's it. That's the whole big scandal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Going from a house, a family, a whole life — to silence and a stranger's walls at midnight. That's a brutal kind of alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It is. I mean — I'm not gonna sit here and cry about it, I'm mostly just pissed off. But some nights it's like... I don't know. It just hits different. You start thinking about things you shouldn't be thinking about at two in the morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What kinds of things?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My kids, mostly. My son had a baseball game last month. I showed up and he just — he barely looked at me. Gave me this little wave. And I'm standing there thinking, is that on me? Did I do that? And then I just... I don't want to think anymore, you know? That's when I really drink. When it gets like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Underneath all that anger at your ex — there's a real fear you might be losing your kids too. And that one's harder to be angry about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter... she used to call me every single night before bed. Every night, for years. And she stopped, maybe two months ago. And I didn't even — I didn't notice right away. One day I just realized and I felt sick. Like, what kind of father doesn't notice that his daughter stopped calling? I just... I felt sick.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What kind of father do you want to be for them? Not who you've been the last four months — who do you want to be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The kind they can count on. The kind that shows up. My dad was... he wasn't around. Or when he was, you wished he wasn't. I swore I'd be different. That was the one thing I told myself. And now I'm in this apartment, drinking scotch alone at eleven on a Tuesday, and I'm thinking — am I him? Am I turning into him?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just say back what I'm hearing, and stop me if I get it wrong. You didn't want to come here. You're here because someone pushed you, and that's fine. You've had your world completely dismantled in four months — the marriage, the house, daily life with your kids. The drinking gets you through the nights. But what's really scaring you isn't the drinking. It's your daughter not calling. Your son barely looking at you. The thought that you might be becoming the thing you promised yourself you never would. That's what's underneath all of this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — I didn't think about it that way exactly, but that's it. That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know, a lot of people in your position would've walked out of here ten minutes ago. You stayed. And you just said something out loud that I'd bet you haven't said to anyone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I thought about leaving. I really did. But... my buddies, they just pour me another drink. They don't — nobody asks me anything real. Maybe I needed someone to just ask me something real. I don't know. I haven't talked. At all. About any of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let's end here with this — six months from now, if things looked different. With your kids, with the drinking, with yourself. What would different actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want my daughter to call again. I want to go to my son's games and have him actually look at me. I want to... I want to be someone they're not embarrassed by. I guess to get there I'd have to — I don't know, get my head right. Maybe that starts here. Maybe. I don't know yet, but... maybe.

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, good to see you again. Honestly, I wasn't sure if you'd come back — that first session can feel like a lot. How's the week been?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... kind of the same, I think? Like I told myself I'd try to cut back and then the baby had a growth spurt or something and wasn't sleeping and I just... yeah. I don't know. It's been a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you went into the week with an intention, and then life kind of had other plans.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. And like... I want to be clear, I'm not drinking to get drunk. It's one, maybe two glasses after she goes down. It's just the only thing that actually works to unwind. Everything else I've tried just doesn't... it doesn't touch it the same way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's doing a job for you that nothing else is doing right now. Almost like a tool you've found that actually works — which makes a lot of sense, even if part of you is uneasy about it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, that's exactly it. And that's kind of what scares me? Because before she was born I'd just watch TV or call a friend and that was enough. Now those things feel like nothing. The wine just works faster and I... I don't love that that's true.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like to notice that shift — that the things that used to be enough aren't anymore?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It feels lonely. Like I'm not the same person I was before she came. And I miss her — the old me. I miss just being able to breathe without feeling like everything is on me all the time. My partner helps but it's still just... it's a lot to carry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back today even though last time was hard. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I have to, right? She's watching me. She doesn't know what she's watching yet but one day she will. My mom drank and I always swore I'd never— (pause) Sorry. I didn't mean to go there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Please don't apologize. That was one of the most important things you've said.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... I already catch myself sometimes, like, just get through dinner, just get her down, and then you can have your glass. And I hear myself thinking it and I'm like — that's not okay. That thought shouldn't be there. I don't want her growing up and wondering why I always had a glass in my hand.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're noticing the thought before you act on it. A lot of people never get to that step — they're halfway through the glass before they even realize what happened. You're already a step ahead of where you think you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought about it like that. I always feel like I'm failing because I still pour it anyway. But... yeah. I do notice it. (pause) I guess that's something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've got the noticing down. What do you think is actually missing in those evenings that makes the wine feel necessary — like what's the gap it's filling?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Connection, maybe? Like my partner tries but he's up at six and by nine he's just done, and I feel like I can't complain because he's doing so much already. But I'm just... alone with it. I think if I had something that was just mine — not the baby, not the house — just something I actually looked forward to, maybe I wouldn't need it as much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something that belongs to you. Not the witching hour, not the feeding schedule — just yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like even twenty minutes. I used to do yoga — I haven't touched it since the third trimester. I was thinking maybe I could just... YouTube it in the living room after she goes down. That probably sounds pathetic but — I don't know, maybe that could be the thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound pathetic — that sounds like someone who knows herself pretty well. You came in today knowing what was scaring you, you figured out what's actually missing, and you came up with something concrete that's yours. I want to reflect that back because I'm not sure you're seeing how much ground you just covered in an hour.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't realize I had all that figured out. (pause) ...Huh. Yeah. Maybe I do.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in. Take whatever seat feels comfortable. There's no rush here — I just want you to know this is your time, and we can go at whatever pace works for you. I'm glad you made it in today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, thanks. Um... I honestly wasn't sure I was gonna come in. I've never done anything like this before. I'm not really a... I don't usually talk to, like, counselors or whatever. My doctor kind of pushed me to come after some lab work came back and I figured, okay, fine, I'll go. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to walk through that door, especially when it's not something you're used to. What was it about those lab results that made today feel like the day to do it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My liver enzymes were elevated. Which my doctor said could mean a bunch of things, you know? Could be nothing. Could be diet, could be — I mean, she asked about drinking and I told her it's, like, casual. I have a couple drinks in the evening, that's... most people do that. But she flagged it anyway and here I am talking to someone about it, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your doctor pointed at the drinking as something worth looking at, and part of you is sitting with that... even if another part of you isn't quite sure there's really a problem here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Kind of. I don't think it's — look, I teach middle school. Do you know what that's like? By three-thirty I've broken up two arguments, answered the same question forty times, and had someone cry in my classroom. I come home, I have a drink, I decompress. That's just... that's just how I function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds genuinely exhausting. The weight you're carrying in that classroom every single day... I don't want to skip past that. And I'm curious — when you say 'a couple drinks,' what does a typical evening actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it... it varies. Maybe three, four beers. Sometimes more if it was a rough day. Sometimes a couple glasses of whiskey instead. I'm not — I'm not drinking in the morning or anything like that. I'm not that guy. I'm functional. I show up, I do my job. Mostly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "Mostly." ...

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — okay, there have been a few mornings where I wasn't exactly... sharp. And a colleague, someone I actually like, she pulled me aside last month and said she was worried. Which was — that was embarrassing. That was really embarrassing. But it's not like she saw me drunk or anything. She just noticed I seemed off. People seem off sometimes. That's not — that doesn't make me an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like that conversation with your colleague really stung. Someone you respect looking at you with concern — that's hard to shake. And you've been carrying all of this: the lab results, her words, the mornings you weren't at your best... and you still showed up here today. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want my kids — my students — to see me like that. That's the thing. I got into teaching because I actually care about these kids. Some of them have nobody in their corner and I'm supposed to be... I'm supposed to be reliable. And lately I've been wondering if I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being in their corner — that's clearly at the core of who you are as a person. What does it feel like when you sit with the idea that the drinking might be getting in the way of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It feels... bad. Like, genuinely bad. I got into this job because my eighth-grade teacher pulled me out of a really dark place and I've always wanted to be that for someone else. And if I'm showing up hungover, or distracted, or whatever... I'm not that. I'm the opposite of that. I don't know when it — I don't know how it got to be every night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I reflect back what I've heard so far, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right? You came in today because your body sent up a flag — your liver, those lab results — and at the same time a colleague who you trust let you know she was worried. The drinking started as a way to get through days that are genuinely hard. But somewhere along the way it became every night, and you've had some mornings that weren't your best, and that gap between the teacher you want to be and where you're at right now... that gap is what's bothering you most.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I haven't actually said all of that out loud before. It sounds worse when you put it together like that. I don't mean that as a criticism, it's just — it's a lot to hear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is a lot. And you're still in the room. Given everything you've just said — who you want to be for those kids, what your body is telling you, what your colleague saw — what do you think you want to do with all of this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I don't want to quit tomorrow and pretend that's easy. But I think I want to understand it better. Like, why is it every night now? Why can't I just — why does one feel like not enough? I never used to be like this. And I think maybe I need to actually look at that instead of just... getting through the week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not asking for a magic fix. You're asking to understand yourself — what's underneath this, what shifted, what you actually need at the end of those hard days. That kind of honesty with yourself is not small. That's where real change actually begins.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't felt hopeful about this until like the last five minutes. Which is weird to say, but... yeah. Maybe I can figure this out. I don't know. But maybe.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, take a seat wherever you want. I'm David. Before we get into anything — nobody's reporting back on what you say in this room. I'm not here to grade you or tell the court how cooperative you were.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I'm gonna be real with you — I don't wanna be here. The judge said I had to come, so I'm here. But I think this whole thing is a joke. I had a few drinks, I drove home, okay? That doesn't make me some kind of alcoholic. The system just decided to make an example out of me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the whole way this played out — being ordered here, the label that feels like it's getting put on you — that feels completely unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It IS unfair. You know how many people are out there driving around hammered every single night and nothing happens? I just got unlucky. Twice. And now I gotta sit in some office and talk about my feelings or whatever. I mean — come on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would you rather be doing right now, on a Thursday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Working. I'm a contractor. I got three jobs backed up and instead I'm here. This is costing me money, actual money, every hour I'm sitting in this chair. Nobody factors that in. Nobody thinks — oh hey, let's consider the financial impact of this on this guy's life. No. They just stamp a paper and send you somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's not just the anger about being here — there are real, concrete things piling up. The lost hours, the income, the work that's waiting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And my license — they suspended it for six months. Six months. I can't get to half my job sites. I got a... I mean, I have a daughter. She's eleven. I got her on weekends. You try figuring out how to do all of that without a license.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned your daughter.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, she — look, it's fine, I'm handling it. My buddy's driving me when I need it. But it's just... it's a lot, okay? Everything at once. The job, the court stuff, making sure I still see her every weekend. It's a lot to deal with.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That really is a full plate. Work backed up, logistics falling apart, making sure your daughter still sees her dad consistently — and all of this legal stuff landed on top of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. And I'm not saying — look, I'm not saying I handled it perfectly, alright? That night, I'd had a rough week. I'm not saying it was a smart call. But I am not some drunk. I'm not that guy who, like, can't function without it. That's not me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're drawing a line there — between the decision you made that night and who you actually are. What does 'that guy' look like in your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... somebody who needs it to get through the day. Who wakes up and the first thing they think about is a drink. That's not me. I go weeks without touching anything. It's just when things stack up, I... I don't know. I cope however I cope, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to recognize that — the difference between your baseline and what happens when the pressure gets high enough. Not a lot of people can name that about themselves.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I never really thought about it that way. I just always figured, you know, everyone does this. But I guess... I mean, not everyone ends up with two DUIs. Right? That's — yeah, okay. I hear that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If nothing changes from here — the way things are right now — what does that look like for you? For your daughter?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I don't want to think about that. If there's a third one — I lose everything. Custody, probably. My contractor's license is already hanging by a thread. And I just... I don't want my daughter looking at me someday and thinking — I don't want her to be ashamed of me. I never wanted that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So even walking in here today furious, even feeling like the whole system screwed you over — underneath all of that, there's a guy who cares about his kid more than just about anything, who works hard, and who is maybe just starting to wonder if there's something here worth actually looking at.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, I'm still pissed about how it all went down. That part's not going away. But... yeah. Maybe. I don't even know what that would look like, but... yeah.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this might not have been your idea, so I want to be upfront — this is your time, not anybody else's. I'm not here to lecture you or tell you what to do. What I'd like to do is just... understand a bit about what's been going on for you lately. Does that sound okay?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure. I mean, I'm here, right? Honestly my sister basically wouldn't let it go until I made the appointment, so. Yeah. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She cares a lot about you, sounds like. What's your sense of what she was worried about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. She thinks I drink too much, which is — look, I'm a third-year PhD student. That's basically a job description. Everyone in my cohort drinks. She doesn't get that world.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like she's applying a standard that just doesn't fit the reality you're living in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, do you know what a third-year review is? My advisor basically told me my last two chapters were — his word was 'unfocused.' Three years of my life and it's... unfocused. So yeah, I'm having a few drinks at night. Sue me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real gut punch. You've put years of serious work into this, and to hear it reduced to one word like that... that would knock anyone sideways.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I'm not — I'm not looking for sympathy. I just... I'm handling it, okay? I come home, I have some drinks, I decompress, and then I get back to work. That's a system. That's literally coping.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And that system matters to you — having something that turns the volume down. What does it actually feel like when you sit down with that drink after a day like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... relief? For a little while my brain just. Stops. The loop of — am I smart enough, why did I even get into this program, what if my advisor's right — it all just goes quiet. And I need that. I genuinely need that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's doing something really important — it's giving you a break from a loop that sounds completely exhausting. And I'm curious, because you said 'for a little while.' What happens after that window closes?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... honestly? I wake up more anxious than when I went to bed. Like I'll feel fine at eleven and then at three AM I'm just wide awake convinced I'm going to get kicked out of the program. And then I'm trying to write hungover and it's... the chapters aren't getting better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to notice about yourself. When you imagine the version of this PhD that you actually wanted — when you applied, when you got in — what did that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wanted to do research that... actually mattered. Like I have this whole chapter on veteran reintegration outcomes that could genuinely inform policy someday. That's why I'm here, that's why I picked this program. I'm not here to just — I don't know. Survive.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You chose this because the work means something to you. That's not nothing — a lot of people lose that thread entirely by year three and you still know exactly why you're here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I do. And I think that's... that's part of why this is so scary? Like if I tank this, I'm not just losing a degree. I'm losing — that version of what I wanted to do. And the drinking is not... it's not helping me get there. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what you've shared, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. You came in because your sister pushed you to, and that felt a little unfair. You've been under real pressure — your advisor's feedback hit hard, and drinking became a way to quiet a mental loop that just won't shut off. But you're also noticing it's not actually working the way you need it to — the anxiety is worse in the mornings, the writing isn't improving. And underneath all of that, there's a really clear sense of purpose that you haven't let go of. The research, the policy impact, the reason you started. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. That's it, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So given all of that — where does it leave you? What feels like it might be worth exploring?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know what that looks like exactly. But I think I need something that actually works. Like I can't keep waking up at three AM and trying to write a dissertation. So. Maybe yeah. Maybe I should figure out something different.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time today — I know you mentioned you're between things. There's no agenda here, no checklist we have to get through. I'm just... genuinely curious about you. How are you doing with all of this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm going to be straight with you. I don't know why I'm here. Dr. Patel flagged something on some questionnaire and suddenly I'm sitting in a — a wellness center. I run a company. Four hundred employees. I don't think I need... this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like this feels a little out of place for you. Like you're the one who solves problems — not the one who gets sent somewhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And I'm not — look, I'm not some person with a problem. I function at an extremely high level. My board is happy, my numbers are up, I just closed a Series C two months ago. If something was actually wrong with me, I would know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think it was that caught Dr. Patel's attention on that questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The drinking questions. How many per week, do you drink alone, has it ever caused problems — I answered honestly. I have a scotch in the evening. I've done it for years and it has never once affected my work. Not once. So if that triggers some algorithm... that's a problem with the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the evening scotch is just... part of how your day ends. And from where you're standing, it's not touching the things that matter to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And you have to understand — do you know what it's like to be responsible for that many people's livelihoods every single day? There is always a fire. Always. The scotch is how I get from the office to being able to sleep. That's all it is. It's not complicated.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It does something real for you — it helps you shift gears. I'm curious... what do you think would happen if it wasn't there one night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Nothing. I could stop anytime. I just — there's no reason to. It's not like I'm hiding bottles or drinking at seven in the morning. A bottle lasts me... a week. Maybe less in a rough week. Plenty of executives do exactly what I do. It's completely normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot — and you've built something real. That matters. I did notice you said 'maybe less in a rough week.' I'm wondering what those weeks look like for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They're just... harder. More calls, more problems. My partner — she doesn't get it. She thinks it's more than it is, and she's probably the one who — I wouldn't be surprised if she said something to Dr. Patel. She's been on my case about this for months.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does she see that worries her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She says I'm... different. In the evenings. That I'm not — she says I'm not really there. And look, I'm tired. I work twelve, fourteen hour days. Of course I'm not going to be sparkly at nine o'clock. That's exhaustion. That's not a drinking problem, that's just... life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's noticing something's shifted in the evenings... and you're not fully dismissing that, even if you think she's reading it wrong.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I don't know. She cried last month. About this. Which is — I wasn't expecting that. She's not dramatic, she doesn't cry about things. So that was... that was something. I didn't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Her crying landed. That meant something to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It did. I just — I don't know if she's right or if she's... I mean, I know I'm not an alcoholic. But also... things have changed. I'm not — I don't know what normal looks like anymore. That's a weird thing to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today saying this wasn't necessary — and somewhere along the way, something shifted. You're not sure what's normal. Your partner is scared. And there's a part of you that doesn't quite know what to do with that. That's actually a really honest place to be. Would it be okay to keep talking — no pressure, just... keep exploring this together?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... maybe. I've got some time next Thursday. I'm not — I'm not promising anything. But yeah. Yeah, okay.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for coming in today. I know this isn't easy — walking through a door like this takes something. I just want you to know there's no agenda here, no script we have to follow. I'm just... I'm really glad you're here. Can you tell me a little about what's going on for you right now, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... honestly? My husband basically made me come. Like, he said if I didn't go to detox and then... do this, he was leaving. So. I don't know if I actually have a real problem or if he's just — I don't know. Overreacting, maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because of him... and another part of you isn't sure you even need to be here at all.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I was drinking, okay, I won't pretend I wasn't. But like — it wasn't like some alcoholic thing. It was just... there was nothing else to do. We moved here almost two years ago and I just — I didn't know anyone. Still don't, really. And he works all the time so... I don't know. The wine made the evenings not feel so long.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The evenings feeling so long... I want to sit with that for a second. What has it actually been like, these two years? Moving somewhere completely new, alone in a lot of ways?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's — god, it's so hard to explain. Back home I had my sister, my friends from university, my mother was close by. Here I just... nobody talks to their neighbors, you know? I tried some groups, like a language exchange thing, but I felt so stupid, my English wasn't — I kept making mistakes and I just stopped going. And then after a while I stopped trying. And then... yeah. I don't know, it crept up. One glass became two became... I don't want to say how much it became.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You tried. You actually put yourself out there, in a language that wasn't yours, in a culture that was unfamiliar, and when it felt too vulnerable you... you found something that numbed that a little. That makes a lot of sense. And I also hear something brave in the fact that you're sitting here talking about all of this right now, after detox, which is — that's not nothing. That is genuinely hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Nobody's really said it like that before. Like, everyone just talked about the drinking. My husband, the detox people — they kept asking about units and triggers and — and I kept thinking, the trigger is that I'm lonely. That's it. That's the whole answer. I miss home so much it's like a physical thing sometimes, like a weight.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A weight. Yeah. Grief can feel like that — and what you're describing, losing your whole world, your people, your sense of belonging... that's a real grief. The drinking didn't come from nowhere. It came from that weight.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought of it as... grief. I just thought I was weak. Like, other people immigrate and they're fine. My cousin came here five years ago and she loves it. I kept thinking, what is wrong with me that I can't just... adjust.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's nothing wrong with you. People grieve differently. People need connection differently. You needed your village, and you didn't have it. That's not weakness — that's being human. I'm curious... when you imagine a life here that actually feels okay, what does that look like? What would have to be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'd have one real friend. Just one. Someone to have coffee with, you know? Someone who'd notice if I was having a bad day. My husband loves me but he doesn't always — he grew up here, he doesn't really understand what it feels like to not belong anywhere. I want to feel like I belong somewhere again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I get it right. You came here today partly because your husband asked you to — but underneath that, there's something very real happening for you. You've been carrying an enormous loneliness, a grief for the life and the people you left behind. The drinking was a way to survive that, not a character flaw. And what you actually want — what's been missing — is connection. One real, honest connection. Does that feel close to the truth?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's exactly it. And I think... I think I stopped believing I could have that here. Like somewhere along the way I just decided this place wasn't for me and I was going to be alone in it forever. And that's when it got really bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And now? Right now, sitting here — is there any part of you that thinks it might not have to stay that way?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Maybe. Like, I don't know, this is the first conversation I've had in months where I didn't feel like I had to explain myself or defend myself or — you know? And I don't even know you. So maybe... maybe I was wrong about this place. Or wrong about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That right there — what you just said — that is not nothing. That is actually a lot. The part of you that believed you were wrong, that gave up... it's still listening. It's still here. And it just let itself be a little bit open, for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to go back to how it was. I really don't. The detox was awful and I was so ashamed the whole time but I also — god, there were other women there who got it, you know? Who understood. And I thought, I've been so stupid, isolating like that. There are people here who would understand me. I just have to find them. I want to find them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked into detox ashamed, and you walked out knowing you're not alone. You walked in here today because someone you love was scared for you, and now you're here because of you — because you want something different. You've shown me so much courage in this hour. I want us to keep doing this work together, and I want to help you find those people, build that one real connection. You deserve to belong somewhere. You deserve that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't cried like this in a long time. I think I've been so scared to feel it that I just... drank instead. But yeah. Yeah, I want to come back. I think I actually want to come back.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know you mentioned you've got class in about forty minutes, so I want to make sure we use your time well. You were referred by your academic advisor — I'm curious, in your own words, what do you think brought you here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I have no idea. She made it sound like some huge thing. I'm passing my classes, I show up, I do what I'm supposed to do. I've been through two deployments — I think I can manage my own life without someone sending me to a counselor.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two deployments — what branch, where?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Army. Afghanistan, twice. So yeah, I've seen things that would break most people, and I'm fine. Having a few drinks to unwind at the end of the day — that's not a problem, that's just... that's just Tuesday. That's what everybody did. That's what you do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's just part of the culture. Normal. Something you've always done alongside the people you trusted most.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. You come back stateside and suddenly everyone's acting like a beer after work is some kind of red flag. It's not. My guys back in the unit — nobody thought twice about it. You work hard, you drink, you move the hell on. I'm not sitting in a ditch somewhere, I'm in college trying to get a degree. That's not what a guy with a problem looks like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And I'm not here to argue with you about what it looks like. I'm genuinely curious — you've got school, you've got all this history behind you. What does a regular week actually look like for you right now? At home, I mean, not just on campus.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's fine. Four classes, which is a lot but I can handle it. Home is... it's been tense lately. My wife, she uh — she's been on my case about a bunch of stuff. But that's a separate thing. That's not what this is about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: School in one box, home in another. Keeping them separate so you can function.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I have to. Because if I — look, she's been threatening to leave. Okay? Take our daughter and leave. And I get it, I understand she's frustrated, but I'm not some... I'm not a drunk. I'm a veteran trying to get a degree so I can actually provide for my family. She should be — I don't know. It feels like nothing I do is ever enough for her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds exhausting — putting in all that work and still feeling like you're coming up short in her eyes. When she says she might leave... what goes through your head in those moments?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I shut down. Or I get pissed and walk out. But then later, when it's quiet and I'm... and I've had some time... I think about my daughter. She's four. And I think, what if she grows up and I'm not — what if I'm not there the way I should be? That scares me more than anything that ever happened over there. And that's saying something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That fear of not being there for her the way she needs — that's a father who loves his kid. That's real.

utterances.speaker: client
