utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, she's... she's everything, man. I just — I don't know how to... I don't want to turn into my dad. He checked out completely when I was growing up. Just gone, even when he was sitting right there. I swore I'd never do that. I swore it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to pull this together, because you've shared a lot. You've got the drinking, which feels normal and honestly earned given what you've been through. You've got the pressure of school, a marriage that's in real trouble, and underneath all of it this fear of repeating a pattern you watched destroy your own childhood. And yet — you almost didn't come in today, and you did anyway. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost sat in my car the whole time. I had my hand on the door handle and I was just... I almost left. But... I don't know. Maybe she has a point. My wife. Maybe I — maybe I don't always see it the way other people see it. I'm not saying she's right about everything. But... maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No pressure, no right answer — but I want to ask you to imagine something. Six months from now, things are actually better at home. With your daughter. What does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd be... present. Like actually there, not just in the same room checked out. My wife and I could actually have a conversation without it blowing up. I'm not saying I'd stop drinking entirely, I'm not going to promise that, but... maybe less. Maybe not every single night. That — that actually sounds like something I could picture. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here ready to be out the door in five minutes, and instead you just named what you're most afraid of and what you actually want. That took guts. So before we wrap up — if there was one small thing, just one, you'd be willing to try before we meet again, what would it be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... on the nights when she's actually trying to talk to me, actually trying — I skip it. The drinking. Just those nights. Be there for real. I'm not promising anything huge, I'm not signing up for rehab or whatever, but... yeah. I can try that. I think I can do that.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you coming in. I know this kind of appointment feels different from a regular clinic visit — less concrete, maybe. There's no agenda I need to push through. Whatever's on your mind.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... my doctor said I needed to come, so here I am. I'm not really a — I don't really do this. Talk to people. About stuff. I'm more of a figure-it-out-yourself kind of guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Figure it out yourself. That's served you for a long time, sounds like. [pause] The labs — what was it like hearing that news from your doctor?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Liver numbers. He got all serious, started drawing stuff on that little paper they put on the exam table. Look, I've been going through a lot lately. My divorce finalized four months ago — twenty-two years. Anyone would drink more. That's just... that's just what happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. And the drinking has been one way of getting through these four months.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah. I'm not an alcoholic, I want to be clear about that. I function fine. Work, the whole thing. It's just... the nights are long. I'm in this apartment now, and it's — it's nothing. It smells like the last guy's dog and there's nothing on the walls and I just... I drink a little to turn the volume down. That's all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Turns the volume down. [pause] What's the volume when it's up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... thoughts. Going over things. Like, what I could've done different, or — I get angry sometimes, really angry at her, and then I feel like an idiot for being angry because that doesn't do anything, and then I just... I miss her. And then I'm angry again. It's like this loop. The drinking breaks the loop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The anger and the missing her — they're almost the same thing. Both of them are about losing something that mattered to you deeply.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...[long pause] My kids are over there. My son — he's seventeen — he called me last Tuesday. Just to talk, I think. And I'd had a few. I wasn't, like, falling down or anything. But I kept losing the thread. He was telling me something about a game, or practice, and I just... [trails off] I could hear it in his voice. That he noticed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You stayed on that call. Even when it was painful. [pause] That tells me something about who you are as a father.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if that counts for much. [voice tightens] I moved into that apartment — I took the worse end of the deal on purpose so the kids could stay in the house, keep their school, their friends. I was trying to do right by them. And somehow I'm still... I don't know. I don't know what I'm doing anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You gave up the house so they wouldn't have to lose anything else. [pause] That wasn't nothing. That was a man who still puts his kids first even when he's hurting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I used to be... I used to be that guy. The one they could count on. I coached little league. I never missed a game. And now I'm — I'm missing phone calls, basically. In my own apartment at nine o'clock on a Tuesday. [exhales sharply] That's not who I wanted to be at forty-eight.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That guy — the one who never missed a game — he's still in there. You're describing him right now. What would it look like to get back to him? Not all at once, just... what would a step in that direction look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Being... actually present when he calls. Not just picking up, but actually being there. I want him to be able to call me about anything and know I'm — that I'm his dad, you know? Solid. I was solid. I don't know how I got so far from that in four months.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I try to pull some of this together? [pause] You came in because of a real health scare — your body sending up a flare. The drinking has been getting you through the longest, loneliest nights you've probably ever had. After losing a marriage, a home, and your daily life with your kids — all at once. That's not weakness. That's a man carrying something enormous. And underneath all of it, what keeps coming through is this: you want to be solid for your son. You still see yourself as his dad first. That's not gone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...[long silence] When you say it like that. [clears throat] I still have time, right? I mean — I'm not so far gone that I can't... I'm forty-eight. My dad was still coaching rec league at sixty. I've got time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got time. [pause] What feels like the right first step — something real, not a list, just one thing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Call him back. Actually call him, sober, and just... ask about the game. And maybe — I don't know — maybe come back here. Talk to you again. That felt like... [small, quiet laugh] I don't know. Less terrible than I thought it would.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So we had a difficult week. You mentioned when you called that something happened at work — I want to hear about all of it, but first just... how are you doing right now, sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm embarrassed. Which I didn't expect to feel walking in here, but... yeah. They're treating it like I committed some kind of crime. I had a rough morning, I was a little off, and now suddenly there's an incident report and HR is involved and — I don't know. It feels like a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in anyway. That matters, even if part of you didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't have much of a choice, did I. They basically said — the EAP referral was... well. It was either this or... I don't know what. But I also — and I know how this sounds — I do think I needed to come back. Last week was bad. Robert's birthday was Tuesday and I just... I didn't handle it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what Tuesday night looked like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay. I had some wine. A bottle, maybe a little more, I'm not going to sit here and lie to you. But it was his birthday. He would've been sixty-two. I ordered from the Italian place we always went to, I sat at the table, and I — it's not like I was out doing something dangerous. I was at home. Alone. I don't see why that's anybody's business.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And then you went into work the next morning, and something was off enough that a colleague noticed and filed a report.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I smelled like wine. Maybe. I don't know. I wasn't stumbling around, I wasn't slurring. I've been a nurse for thirty years and I never once compromised patient care. Never. One bad morning and suddenly I'm... what, a liability? I've given that hospital everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thirty years. That's not nothing — that's your whole identity, your whole sense of who you are. And right now it feels like the one place that was still solid is also starting to shift underneath you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's actually exactly what it feels like. Because Robert is gone, and my kids are doing their own things, which is fine, they have lives, I'm not going to be that mother. And work was the one thing I still had. And now even that feels — God, I don't know. Shaky.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been holding a lot, alone, for eight months. And the wine — it's not that it doesn't make sense. It quiets something down at night when the house gets too quiet. The question I keep coming back to is: is it actually helping you carry the weight, or is it just making the weight harder to feel for a few hours?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't sleep without it anymore. That's... that's probably something, isn't it. I used to sleep fine. I'd read, I'd fall asleep by ten. Now I'm up until two, three in the morning and the only way I — I mean, I know that. I do know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think Robert would make of how you're living right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, he'd be furious with me. [laughs softly, then stops] He'd — he'd sit right down next to me and say 'Margaret, what are you doing.' Not mean about it. Just... he never raised his voice. He'd look at me and I'd know. He was so steady. I'm not steady without him. I don't know how to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it's important. You lost Robert — your steadiness, your person — eight months ago. You've been trying to get through it alone, keeping it together for your kids, showing up for your patients. And the drinking started quietly, to get through the nights, but now it's costing you sleep, it's showing up at work, and somewhere underneath the frustration about that incident report, you already know something has to change. That's not me saying it — that's you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... [pause] I'm so tired. I'm really, really tired. Not of being here, I don't mean it like that — just tired of managing. Of pretending I'm fine. I'm not fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Saying that out loud — 'I'm not fine' — that takes something real. What would feeling even a little more okay actually look like for you? Not fixed, not back to how things were. Just... less like this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sleeping. Just... sleeping through the night without needing anything. Maybe calling my daughter — I've been putting that off because I don't want her to worry, but I think she already knows something's wrong. And maybe coming back here. Talking to someone who doesn't look at me like I'm broken.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here embarrassed, and you're leaving having named things out loud that you haven't said to anyone. That's not small, Margaret. The sleep, the call to your daughter, coming back — those are real, concrete things. We can build from there. You don't have to figure out the whole rest of it today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I can do those things. I think — yeah. I think I actually can.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for making time today. I know telehealth can feel a little different — being in your own space. So, what's going on? What made you decide to reach out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm still kind of figuring that out. Like, I don't — I mean, I'm fine. I really am. My friend Becca basically ambushed me with like a whole intervention thing at brunch last month, and it's just been... sitting with me, I guess. But I want to be upfront — I don't think I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So something Becca said actually got through — even if you're not sure what to make of it yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... sort of? She was crying, which — Becca doesn't cry, so that was weird. But she also has a tendency to catastrophize, you know? She's always been the anxious one in our group. I love her to death but she sees drama where there isn't any. I just like to have fun. That's literally my brand.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's your brand. And I'm curious — when you said it's been sitting with you, what exactly has been sitting with you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay so — and this is not a big deal — I had this sponsored event in January, like a rooftop collab thing, and I... I don't remember all of it. Which happens sometimes, right? It's not — I've seen it happen to plenty of people. But there were photos that went up and I looked really out of it, and the comments were... not great. I deleted the post but people screenshot everything so. That was a moment.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like it really rattled you — losing a chunk of a professional event, and then seeing yourself through other people's eyes like that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Rattled is a strong word. It was uncomfortable. I've worked really hard on my image — like, years of work. And for one night to potentially undo some of that? That sucked. But I handled it. I did a whole candid morning routine post the next day, very minimal makeup, very 'I'm just a real person' energy, and it totally redirected the narrative. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're clearly very good at managing how things look on the outside. I'm wondering — what's it like on the inside, when you're not managing the narrative?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. That's kind of a weird question. Um. I'm always kind of 'on,' I guess? Even at home I'm thinking about content — what to post, what not to post, who's tagging me in what. It's a lot. And drinking is just... it helps me turn that off for a bit. Is that so bad?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It quiets something that never really gets to quiet down on its own.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. I mean... god, when you say it like that it sounds sad. It's not sad. I have a genuinely great life, I love my life. It's just — sometimes it's a lot to hold. But I'm not like... I'm not an alcoholic or whatever. I don't drink alone. I don't drink in the mornings. I have rules.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You have rules. And you've also blacked out at a work event and had your closest friend crying at brunch. What do you make of that gap — between the rules and what's actually been happening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know. I mean. Maybe I've moved the goalposts a few times without really noticing. Like there was a point where I wouldn't drink before 6 PM and now it's like, if there's a mimosa situation at brunch, obviously that's different — that's just brunch. But I hear what you're saying. I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You're someone who runs her own brand, who's incredibly attuned to how she's perceived, and who is never really off. You reached out because something Becca said got through, and because there was a night that scared you — even if 'scared' isn't the word you'd pick. And underneath all of that, you're describing using alcohol to get a break from a life that doesn't have an off switch. Does that feel close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. That's — yeah. That's pretty close. I don't love hearing it but... yeah. I booked this appointment at like 2 AM. I'd been scrolling through those screenshots again. So. I think that tells you something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It does. Being up at 2 AM with something hard and actually doing something about it instead of just scrolling past it — that took real courage. So let me ask you this: setting aside what anyone else thinks — Becca, your followers, me — what do you actually want for yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to feel like I'm in control again. Like I'm choosing things instead of just... ending up in them. I don't want to black out. I don't want Becca to look at me like that again. And honestly? I want to wake up and not immediately check if I did something embarrassing the night before. That would be really nice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's really clear. And those aren't small things — that's you telling me what you actually value, underneath all of it. Control. Presence. Peace of mind. You showed up today, and I think you know more than you're letting yourself admit yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I'm not ready to say I have a problem out loud. But I'm... I'm open to figuring out what's actually going on. Which is probably the most honest thing I've said in a while, so. That's something, right?

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I know last week wasn't easy, and... I want to start by just checking in — how are you doing today? Not the court-required answer. Just... how are you actually doing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: How am I doing? Are you serious right now? I had to leave work early again, my boss is already breathing down my neck, and I'm sitting here because some judge decided this is how I'm gonna spend my Thursday afternoons. So... yeah. I'm great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The whole thing feels like it's been dropped on you. Like none of this was your choice.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It wasn't. I mean — look, I know what you're gonna say. 'Oh but you chose to drive.' Yeah, okay, fine. But a .09? That's basically nothing. Half the people on that highway had more in 'em than I did. The system just... it's rigged for people like me. Working guys who don't have fancy lawyers.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. I hear that — the unfairness feels real. And... I just want to say something. You didn't have to come back today. A lot of people don't. But here you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well... court says I gotta or I lose my license permanently. So don't read too much into it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The lab work from last month — your liver numbers came back off. You mentioned it kind of in passing right at the end of last session. I've been sitting with that all week. What has it been like for you, carrying that around?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's probably nothing. My doctor's been on my case about drinking for years, they always find something to worry about. Elevated this, elevated that. I don't sleep great, I eat like crap — it could be a hundred things. I'm not some kind of... I'm not an alcoholic, if that's what you're implying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't see yourself that way. And at the same time... something about those numbers stuck with you enough to bring them up, even when you were halfway out the door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I don't know. My dad, he — he had liver problems. Real bad. By the time they caught it he was already... [pause] ...I'm not my dad. I just — the numbers caught me off guard, that's all. I wasn't expecting that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I don't want to rush past that. When you think about your dad — and then you look down at that piece of paper with those numbers on it — what goes through you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I got two kids. Eight and eleven. And I think about... I don't know. I'm not ready to — I'm not saying it's that serious, I just. They need me around. Their mom and I aren't together anymore so it's like... I'm it, you know? I'm what they got.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're it. That's... that's not a small thing to carry.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And the thing is — and I don't do this a lot, apparently — when I'm actually honest with myself... I know I've been drinking more since the divorce. Like, significantly more. After the kids go back to their mom's, the quiet just... it gets really loud. And the drinking makes it quiet again. That's the only way I can describe it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just try to hold everything you've shared today, because I think it matters. You came back, even when part of you didn't want to. You're furious at being here — and that makes sense, it feels like the system has its boot on your neck. And underneath all of that, there's a man who watched his father get sick. Who knows, when he's being honest, that something has shifted. Who has two kids he doesn't want to let down. And who is drinking to get quiet in a house that got very empty very fast.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...when you say it like that it sounds... I don't know. It sounds worse than I let myself think about. Like when it's all just... out there like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying a lot of this by yourself. And I think it takes real courage — not the fake kind, the actual kind — to sit in that and let yourself hear it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I'd call it courage. I just... I think I'm tired, man. I'm tired of being angry all the time. Tired of waking up feeling like garbage. Maybe... I don't know. Maybe something has to change. I haven't really let myself say that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something has to change. You said that. Not me — you. And I want you to just sit with that for a second... because that's you, talking to yourself. What does it feel like to say that out loud?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Scary. But also... I don't know. Like maybe there's actually something on the other side of this. I never let myself think that far. Usually I just get mad and shut it down. But... maybe. I don't know. Maybe.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Gerald, can you hear me okay? Good. Thanks for joining — I know doing this over video probably wasn't exactly on your retirement bucket list. So, look, I know you're here because the court said you had to be, and I just want to be upfront: I'm not here to lecture you or check a box. What's on your mind coming into today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think this is a load of... I mean, one mistake. One. And now I gotta talk to a — no offense — a stranger on a computer screen every week. I'm sixty-five years old. I didn't need babysitting when I was thirty and I sure as hell don't need it now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: None taken. And yeah — sixty-five years of figuring things out on your own, and now some judge says you need to check in with someone. That would tick me off too, honestly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. It really does. And my doctor's in on it now too — liver this, liver that. Like, I have a couple drinks in the evening to unwind, what's the big crime? My father drank his whole life and he lived to eighty-two. Nobody sent him to therapy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it feels like everyone's ganging up — the court, the doctor... what actually happened the night that got you in front of a judge? If you don't mind me asking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... drove. Shouldn't have. I know that. I'm not stupid. But it was — it was late, I'd had a few, I just needed to get to the pharmacy and it was one mile, maybe less. Cop was waiting right there. Almost like he knew. And now here we are.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You knew it wasn't a good call, even as you were making it. That's actually — that matters, Gerald. That kind of self-awareness isn't nothing. But I'm also hearing that something had you up late, needing to go out. What was going on that night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Nothing. Everything. I just... I couldn't sleep. Again. I sit in that house and it's just — quiet. Too quiet. My wife passed four years ago, my kids are in different states, and I retired two years back thinking, great, finally some peace. But it's not peace. It's just... empty.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot of loss hitting at once — your wife, your work, the structure that probably kept your days from feeling like that. When you retired, what did you think it was going to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I thought I'd... travel, maybe. Do the things you put off when you're working. But then Carol got sick, and then she was gone, and I just — I didn't do any of it. And now I'm just rattling around in a house that's way too big for one person. The drinking... it takes the edge off. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It quiets things down. The house, the thoughts, the feeling of — what, like the days don't have a shape anymore?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it, actually. No shape. I wake up and there's nothing I have to do. Which sounds great, right? God, I used to dream about that. But it's — I don't know. It feels like I'm just waiting. And I don't even know what I'm waiting for.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Gerald, I want to say something. You came in here ready to fight, which — fair enough, I get it. But in about ten minutes you've gone somewhere most people take months to get to. That kind of honesty with yourself? That's not easy. A lot of guys your age would've just stonewalled me the whole hour.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Well. I'm not most guys. Ha. I don't know, maybe I've been waiting to say some of this out loud. My son calls once a week but you can't — you can't dump all this on your kid, you know? He's got his own life. I don't want to be a burden.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I'm off base. You lost Carol. You retired. You had this picture of what those years were supposed to look like, and it didn't match reality. The drinking started filling the space — taking the edge off the quiet, helping you sleep, getting through evenings alone. And somewhere along the way it's become more than a couple drinks, and your body and the law are both starting to flag it. But underneath all of that, there's a guy who still knows what he wants — he just hasn't found it yet since everything changed. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, it does. I didn't think I'd be sitting here at sixty-five feeling like I'm starting over. That feels embarrassing to say. But yeah, that's... that's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nothing embarrassing about it. Starting over at sixty-five is harder and rarer than people think — most people just don't. So I have to ask: if the drinking weren't in the picture, if we dealt with that piece, what would you actually want the next chapter to look like? What would give the days a shape again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hm. I used to woodwork. Before Carol got sick I had a whole shop set up in the garage. Haven't touched it in... four, five years. And there's a veterans' group at the community center — my neighbor keeps mentioning it. I always brush him off. I don't know why. Maybe I'm scared it'll be depressing. But... I think about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The shop's still there. The group's still there. And you're still thinking about them — that tells me something, Gerald. That part of you hasn't gone anywhere. You came in today ready to do your time and get out. Instead you just handed me a roadmap. I think we've got something real to work with here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe so. I'm not gonna pretend this is gonna be easy or that I'm suddenly some changed man after one session. But... yeah. Maybe so. I'll come back next week. We'll see how it goes.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time for this today. I know the session was set up through your employer, which isn't always how people choose to start these conversations. So — how are you feeling about being here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's fine. I don't really know what to expect. My manager said I had to do this, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because you had to be, and you're not sure what this is going to look like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I just — I don't think there's some big problem or whatever. There was an incident at work, yes, but it was one time. I was having a really rough week and I had a couple drinks at lunch and someone noticed. That's it. I'm not like... I don't have a drinking problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. That sounds like it was a genuinely hard week. Can you tell me a bit about what that week looked like for you — what was going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... it's been a rough few months, honestly. I moved here — to Canada — about eighteen months ago, and it's just. It's harder than I thought it would be. I don't really have anyone here. My family is back home in India, totally different time zones, it's not easy to just call, and I work a lot, and when I come home it's just... quiet. Really quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eighteen months of quiet. That's a long time to be carrying that alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — I knew it would be hard, I'm not naive. But I guess I didn't expect it to feel like I just... disappear when I leave the office. Like nobody knows I exist. Back home there was always someone knocking on your door — a neighbor, your auntie, someone. Here it's just... nothing. You close the door and that's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feeling of disappearing — what does that do to you in those evenings when you get home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I started drinking more. I know that's probably what you want me to say. At first it was just like, a glass of wine to unwind, which is normal, right? But now it's... I don't even know. I open a bottle when I get home and it's just gone by the time I go to sleep. It kind of makes the silence... bearable, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just named something really honest — that it's not about the taste or even relaxing after work. It's about making the silence bearable. That takes a lot of self-awareness to see that clearly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... I don't like saying it out loud, because then it sounds like a problem. And I keep telling myself, like, once I make some friends here, once things get better, I'll just stop. I don't need to do this forever. It's just... for now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you already has a picture of what life looks like without needing to drink through the evenings. What would be different about that version of your life — the one where things are better?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd feel more like myself. Like the person I was back home. I used to go dancing with my friends, I used to cook big meals for people, I was — I was fun. I was loud. I miss that person. She feels very, very far away right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The loud, dancing, cooking person — she's not gone. You moved across the world alone, held down a job for eighteen months in a country where you knew nobody, and kept going. That person has been here the whole time. She's just been surviving.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... that actually made me want to cry a little. I think I've been so focused on just getting through each day that I forgot I'm allowed to actually live here. Like actually build a life. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes complete sense. The connection piece is clearly really central to who you are. Have you come across any spaces here — even small ones — where you've felt even a little bit like yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There's this South Asian cultural association in the city — I got an email about them months ago and I just... never went. I don't know why. Maybe I was scared, or maybe — I think if I made friends here it meant I was really staying, and I'm not sure I'm ready to admit that I'm staying. That this is my life now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard today. You came in here because your employer required it — not by choice. But in one conversation, you've connected the drinking directly to real loneliness, not a character flaw. You've told me exactly who you want to be again. And you mentioned a door that's been sitting there for months — a community email you haven't opened yet — not because you don't want to, but because wanting it meant making this life real. That's not avoidance. That's someone who is very close to being ready.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. Yeah, I think I might actually be ready. I'm tired of just surviving. And maybe I don't have to fix everything at once — maybe I just go to one event. Or I call my mom even if the time zone is terrible. I don't know, it just feels... less impossible than it did an hour ago.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for joining me today, Marcus. I know this is a telehealth session so you're at home — hopefully that feels a little more comfortable. I want to be upfront: I'm not here to lecture you or tell you what to do. My job is just to understand what's going on for you. So, in your own words... what do you know about why you're here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my mom basically forced me to do this. She heard about what happened at Kyle's party and she just — she freaked out. Like, completely overreacted. I'm 21, I'm in college, this is just... this is what people do. I don't actually have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it sounds like this whole thing feels pretty unfair to you — like you got pulled into this because of someone else's reaction, not because you think anything's actually wrong.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. Like, everyone drinks in college. Every single one of my friends does the same stuff I do, more even, and nobody's dragging them to therapy. It's like... I got singled out because my mom panicked and now I'm the problem. It's bullshit. Sorry — I mean, it's frustrating.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to apologize. You're frustrated — that comes through clearly. And I hear you: from where you're standing, you look around and see everyone doing the same thing, and you're the one sitting here. That's a real feeling.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And then my friends — some of them did this whole, like, intervention thing last month. Which was just... I don't even know what that was. That pissed me off more than anything. They sat me down like I'm some kind of addict. I was so angry I almost just walked out. Who does that? We're 21.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment with your friends — being sat down like that — it sounds like it felt like a real betrayal. Like people you trusted suddenly turned it into something bigger than it was. What do you think was going through their heads when they did that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, man. I honestly don't. Maybe they were trying to... I don't know, help or whatever. But it didn't feel like help. It felt like they were ganging up on me. And half those guys drink just as much as I do, so who are they to say anything? It's like, mind your own business.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you wonders if they were genuinely worried... even if the way they did it felt all wrong.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess. Maybe. I don't know. It's just — it's like nobody's willing to believe me when I say I'm fine. And that's... that gets exhausting after a while. My mom, my friends, now this. Like, how many times do I have to say it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds draining — to keep feeling like no one's actually listening to your side of it. I'm curious about something, and you don't have to answer if you don't want to. But when you think about what you want your life to look like after graduation... what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I want to get a good job, obviously. I'm applying to some tech companies right now, actually. And like, settle down eventually, I guess. Normal stuff. What does that have to do with anything?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just pause and reflect back what I'm hearing, because I want to make sure I've got it right. You came into this feeling like it was forced on you — your mom panicked, your friends overstepped, and you've been put in a position of defending yourself to everyone. At the same time, you've got real goals: you're job hunting, you're thinking about the future. And underneath all of this frustration, there might be just a little piece of you that's at least... wondering why all these people around you are worried. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I mean. Yeah, kind of. I don't think they're right. But... yeah, I've thought about it. Like, why does everyone keep making it a thing. That question does pop up sometimes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That question keeps coming back, even when you push it away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sometimes, yeah. Like... there was one morning after a party last semester where I just — I felt terrible, and I missed a really important interview prep thing, and I remember thinking like, huh. That sucked. But then it passed and I figured it was just a one-time thing. I'm not going to let that ruin senior year.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That morning clearly stuck with you enough that you still remember it. What was it about that specific moment that made you think 'huh' — even just for a second?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I guess it was the first time I was like, okay, this actually cost me something. Not just a headache, but like an actual thing I needed to do. And the job stuff is serious, I actually care about that. I worked really hard to get to where I am academically. I don't want to mess that up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That matters — and it says something real about you that you can hold that. You've put genuine work into your future, and somewhere in you there's a part that doesn't want drinking to get in the way of that. I'm not going to tell you what to do with that. But I'm glad you said it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I'm still not saying I have a problem. I just — I don't know. Maybe there's stuff worth thinking about. I don't know.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi, I'm really glad you came in today. I know it can feel a little strange, walking into a place like this for the first time. There's no agenda here — we can just... talk. Whatever feels okay to share.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... thanks. It's — yeah, it's a little weird. My advisor kind of nudged me to come, which, I don't know, that felt kind of embarrassing? Like, I'm not... I didn't think I was the kind of person who needed this. But here I am, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here you are. And I'm curious — what's been going on for you lately? In your own words, just... whatever comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm just... tired. I paint, that's what I do, that's who I am. And I've always had a glass or two while I work — like, that's just part of my process, it kind of loosens something up in me. I don't think it's a big deal. I think my advisor just got worried because I've been, like, missing some deadlines for my studio space renewal and stuff. But that's not really... I mean, that's not a drinking thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So drinking is really woven into how you create — it's not separate from your art, it's almost part of the ritual. And at the same time, something has been feeling off enough that you're... tired.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. The thing is, lately the work just — it's not good. Like, I can feel it when I'm making it, there's this moment where I look at the canvas and I think, this is garbage. And I don't know if that's the alcohol or if that's just... me. Like, maybe I was never as good as I thought. That's kind of the scarier thought, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you look at the canvas and it feels like garbage... what does that feel like, in your body, in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Empty. Like this sort of... hollow thud. I used to finish a piece and feel this aliveness, you know? Even if it wasn't perfect, there was this thing. And now I finish something and I just — I pour another drink and I go to bed and I don't look at it again. I had a show last spring and I stood next to my own work and I felt ashamed. I've never felt that before. Not like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Standing next to your own paintings and feeling ashamed. That's a real kind of grief — losing the connection to something that's been such a core part of who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It is. It really is. I don't talk about it because it sounds so dramatic, like, oh, my art isn't good anymore, poor me. But it feels like losing a friend, kind of. Or like — losing myself, I guess. And I don't even know if quitting drinking would bring it back. Maybe nothing would. Maybe this is just who I am now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to ask you something, and take your time with it. What was your relationship with making art like... before drinking became such a big part of your process? What do you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Um... I remember being really intentional. Like, I'd spend an hour just looking at a blank canvas. Not in an anxious way — in a... patient way. I was present. I started drinking to kind of skip past that stillness because it started to feel uncomfortable, and the alcohol made it easier to just go. But now I need it to go anywhere at all. I can't — I literally cannot start a piece sober. That's not... I mean. That feels bad to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It does feel significant to say out loud. And what I'm hearing is something almost like a paradox — you started drinking to unlock your creativity, to get past the block. But somewhere along the way, it became the block.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Huh. I've never — I never thought of it like that. I always thought the drinking was the solution. Like, that was the thing keeping me functioning as an artist. But what you're saying is... maybe I've been solving a problem that the drinking itself created? Is that — am I understanding that right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's exactly it. And the fact that you just named that — that took real honesty. A lot of people go years without letting themselves see that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's terrifying, though. Because if the alcohol isn't what makes me an artist... I don't know what I am without it. Like, I've built this whole identity around it — the tortured creative who drinks, you know? That's — that's the story I've been telling. And if that's not true, then... what's left? Who am I?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine making art differently — not necessarily tomorrow, not perfectly — but in some other way... what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think about mornings. I used to get up really early, before I started drinking at night, and I'd just sit and draw. Nothing planned, no pressure. Just me and a sketchbook and bad coffee. I kind of... I miss that person. That version of me. I don't know where she went but I miss her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to gather what you've shared today, and you can tell me if this feels right. You came in feeling uncertain — not even sure you belonged here. But as we talked, something opened up. You described a kind of grief, losing that alive feeling in your work, standing next to your own paintings and not recognizing yourself in them. And then you did something really courageous — you questioned the story you've been holding. That alcohol is what makes you an artist. And underneath that story, there's a woman who woke up early, sat with a blank page, and trusted herself. She's still in there somewhere. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's it exactly. I think I've been so scared to look at this that I just kept pouring another glass instead. But I think I want to find her again. That morning person. I don't know how yet, but... I think I want to try.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Welcome back. I know last week was difficult, and I want you to know I'm glad you came in today. Before we get into anything, I just want to check — how are you feeling right now, coming through that door?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not great. I almost didn't come. I don't... I don't really see the point sometimes. I had a terrible week and I drank more than I planned to and I already know you're going to say something about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're walking in already bracing for judgment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Kind of, yeah. I mean — I know what I did. I don't need someone to list it back to me. I already feel like garbage. That's the whole thing, I feel bad and then I drink because I feel bad and then I feel worse and it's just... whatever. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear that cycle you're describing. I'm not here to add to the pile. Can you walk me through what actually happened this week — what led up to it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I called my mom. Which sounds stupid, like that shouldn't be a trigger or whatever, but she was asking again when I'm coming back home and I had to explain — again — that I'm not. And she just sounded... sad. Not angry, just sad. And I hung up and the apartment was so quiet. It's always quiet but that night it was like... unbearable. And I didn't know what to do with that so I just — I opened a bottle. And then another one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of quiet after a call like that — your mum sounding sad, not angry — that's its own kind of heavy. You were sitting with something really painful, completely alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... it wasn't even a fight. Somehow that makes it worse, I think. And I don't have anyone here to even just — I don't know, sit with me after something like that. My coworkers are nice but they're not... they're not my people. I don't have people here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say you don't have people here — I want to sit with that for a second. What would it mean to you if you did? If there was someone you could actually call after a night like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I haven't really thought about it that way. I guess it would feel like I actually live here. Like this is my life. Right now it feels like I'm just... passing through. Like everything is temporary, even though it's been two years. That's kind of embarrassing to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're surviving here, not living here. And some part of you wants more than that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think so. I just — I don't know how you make friends as an adult. Back home it just... happened. Here everyone already has their lives. Their groups. I feel like I missed some window and I didn't even know it was open.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I've got it right. You had a painful call with your mum, you were completely alone with nowhere to put that pain, and drinking was the only thing that made the silence bearable. And underneath all of that — what you're really naming — is that you want to actually belong here. Not just exist here. Like this is your life, not a waiting room.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... the waiting room. Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly it. I've never heard it put that way but that's — that's what it feels like every day. A waiting room.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would one small step toward feeling like you actually live here look like? It doesn't have to be big. Just one thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There's... okay, this is going to sound dumb. But I've walked past these flyers a few times for like a cultural association. People from my region who live here. And I keep telling myself I don't need it, but honestly I think I was scared. Like what if I go and even they don't want me? Then I really have no one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You noticed those flyers. You kept walking past them, but you noticed them. Some part of you was looking for a way in, even when another part was too scared to try. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... I mean, it feels like such a small thing. But also kind of — I don't know — like maybe it's something I could actually do. Without it feeling like too much. Which is rare for me right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would make it more concrete — what would help you actually follow through on that, rather than leaving it as a someday?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably just... actually looking up when they meet. Instead of leaving it vague. I do that — I make things vague on purpose I think, so I don't have to commit. And then I say someday, and then I pour a drink instead. So. Maybe I just look it up tonight. Before the quiet gets too loud.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for coming in. I know walking into a place like this can feel... a little strange, honestly. There's no agenda here — I'm not here to lecture you or tell you what you did wrong. Can you just tell me a little bit about what's on your mind today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't really know why I'm here. My mom basically made me come after everything that happened. But it's not like — I don't have a problem or anything. Lots of people drink. Like literally everyone at my school does it, so I don't really get why I'm the one sitting here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it doesn't quite feel like it should be a big deal — but here you are anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I got caught at a school thing and everyone acted like I was some kind of... addict or something. It's so unfair. My friend Mia does it way more than me and nobody dragged her to see a counselor. Like why am I the example all of a sudden?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It really stings to feel singled out like that... I did want to ask — and feel free to tell me if it's too much — but you were in the ER yesterday. That must have been pretty intense. What was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I mean, it was whatever. I just had too much I guess. They put an IV in me and monitored me for a few hours and sent me home. It wasn't like some huge dramatic thing. People get taken to the ER all the time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're saying it wasn't a huge dramatic thing... and at the same time, you woke up in a hospital with an IV in your arm. That's a really scary place to find yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I guess it was kind of scary. Like I didn't really know where I was at first and... um... my mom was just sitting there in the chair next to me. Crying. That was actually the worst part. I kind of wish I hadn't seen that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your mom was crying. What was it like, seeing her like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I felt... bad. Like really bad. I know she was scared and I did that to her. But also I was kind of mad? Which sounds horrible, I know. I just — I wasn't trying to end up there. I just wanted to have fun like everyone else. I didn't mean for any of it to happen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just wanted to belong — to be a regular teenager having a good night. And instead you woke up somewhere frightening, and the person who loves you most was sitting there scared out of her mind.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. That's — yeah. I've been trying so hard to just fit in, you know? Like everyone else makes it look so easy and I always end up going too far or something. And honestly? I don't even like how it feels half the time. Like, I don't know why I keep doing it if I don't even like it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't even like how it feels half the time. I want to stay with that for a second — what does it actually feel like, when you're in those moments?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... kind of numb I guess. For a little while it's fun and I feel like I'm actually part of things. But then it gets weird and I lose track and... the next day I feel gross. And embarrassed, like I said or did something I can't really remember. I don't want to keep feeling like that. I'm kind of tired of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've already noticed something really important — that what you're getting out of it doesn't match what you were hoping for. And the fact that you can see that, and say it out loud? That takes real honesty with yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess I knew something was off for a while. I just never actually said it out loud before. It sounds different when you hear yourself say it. Like maybe I was just... trying really hard not to think about it too much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I just take a moment to reflect back what I'm hearing, if that's okay? You came in today not really sure why you were here, feeling like you'd been unfairly singled out. And somewhere along the way in this conversation, you've also talked about waking up scared in a hospital, watching your mom cry, trying so hard to fit in... and realizing that it hasn't actually been giving you what you were looking for. That's a lot to be sitting with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. When you put it all together like that it's kind of a lot, isn't it. I think I've just been going day by day, not letting myself look at the whole picture. Because if I did I'd have to actually deal with it, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you — to start letting yourself look at the whole picture, even just a little bit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... maybe it would be okay? Like things don't have to keep going the way they have been. I don't really know what that looks like yet but... I think I actually want to figure it out. I don't want to end up in the ER again. I really don't.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I want you to know — a lot of guys don't make it to a second session. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm here, aren't I. My wife basically issued an ultimatum so... here I am. I still don't really see the point of this, to be straight with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like for you, ending up in the ER the other night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was nothing. I had a few too many, blacked out, Sarah panicked and called 911. Whole thing was embarrassing, honestly. Guys I served with would've laughed that off over breakfast.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're standing, this whole situation got blown way out of proportion.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I drank worse overseas and nobody batted an eye — that's just... that's the culture, man. You're downrange, you're under pressure, you come home, you decompress. You drink. It's not some — it's not a disorder. It's just what people do. What we do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me a little about what coming home was like. After the last deployment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I don't know. Fine. Hard, whatever. I really don't want to get into all that. What does any of that have to do with me being in the ER?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to go anywhere you're not ready to go. I'll follow your lead on that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Okay. Look. I'm just saying — I'm not broken, alright? I did my job. I came home. I'm not some... I function. I go to work. I drink like everyone else I know from my unit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And at the same time, something put you in the ER. And you're sitting here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... Sarah said she'd leave. Take Caleb and Emma with her. That's — I mean, that's the only reason I'm in this chair. Let's just be honest about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Of course she does. I'm not — yes. She matters. The kids matter. I just... I don't know what she wants from me anymore. I've given everything. Everything. And somehow I'm still the problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like — in your mind — if things at home were actually okay?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... like before. Before my last deployment. We used to just — we'd sit out on the back porch, I'd have a beer, she'd have her wine, kids would be running around in the yard. That was normal. That was good. Now it's just... every time I crack a beer she looks at me like I'm holding a grenade.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a version of you — the guy on the back porch — that you miss. And it sounds like part of you wonders if he's still in there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Maybe. I don't know if I know how to be that guy anymore, but... I don't want to lose her. I don't want my kids growing up thinking their dad is — you know. Whatever. Some kind of cautionary tale.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm hearing you right. You came in today skeptical — and honestly, that makes complete sense given everything. Part of you still feels like this situation got blown up bigger than it is, and that the way you've been drinking is just normal given what you've been through. But there's another part — the part that keeps showing up here — that doesn't want to lose Sarah, doesn't want to lose the kids, and misses the guy he was before deployment. Both of those things can be true at the same time. That's where you are right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's — yeah. That's pretty much it.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, glad you made it in. I know you mentioned you're squeezed between classes so we can keep this pretty low-key. No agenda on my end. What brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my friends basically made a whole thing out of it. Like they sat me down and were all 'we're worried about you' and whatever. So I guess I'm here because of that. I honestly don't even think there's anything to talk about but like, here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you showed up, even though you're not totally sold on there being a reason to. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I just — I don't want them to keep freaking out, you know? Like it stresses me out. My roommate was literally crying and I'm like... okay, that's a lot. I didn't realize it was such a big deal to them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What did they actually say when they sat you down? Like what was the thing that got your roommate that upset?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said she had to — she had to basically take care of me two weekends ago because I threw up and couldn't really walk straight. And apparently I said some stuff I don't remember saying. But I mean that was one night, that's not... that happens to everyone at a party. She made it sound like I'm some kind of alcoholic which is just insane.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There were things you said that you don't remember saying.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah but — okay, I was really drunk. That's just what happens when you drink a lot. It's not like I do that every single week. And besides, it was a huge party, everyone was going hard that night. It wasn't just me by a long shot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sounds like you feel like you're being singled out for something that's pretty normal in your world.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly! Like yes, thank you. Everyone at this school drinks on weekends. I have a good GPA, I go to class, I'm not failing out or whatever. What's the actual problem here? I just — I genuinely don't get why I'm the one sitting in a counselor's office.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you. So let me ask you something — and there's no right answer — what would drinking have to look like for you to think, okay, maybe there's something worth looking at here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... like if I was drinking during the week? Or missing class because of it? I don't do any of that. I only drink on weekends. I have like, rules for myself. It's not like I'm sitting alone in my room with a bottle of vodka on a Tuesday night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got lines you've drawn for yourself — things you'd never cross. And at the same time, there's this moment that you can't fully account for. Words you don't remember, someone who cares about you in tears. Both of those things are sitting next to each other right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...
Yeah.
I mean... she's been my best friend since freshman year. And she was looking at me like she was scared of me. Like genuinely scared. That kind of... I don't know. That kind of messed me up a little bit if I'm being honest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like seeing that look on her face?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It sucked. It really sucked. Like... I don't want to be that guy. I don't want my friends walking on eggshells around me or whatever. I just — I don't think I am that guy. But I guess maybe sometimes I... I don't know. Maybe sometimes it gets away from me a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something I don't think was easy to say. That sometimes it gets away from you. That's actually a pretty honest thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — I'm still not saying I have a problem, I want to be clear about that. But I... yeah. I don't want to hurt my friends. That's not — that's not who I'm trying to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So here's what I'm hearing. You came in skeptical, and you're still not ready to put a label on any of this. And at the same time, something happened that you can't fully shake — a friend who looked scared, words you can't account for, a version of yourself that doesn't line up with who you want to be. You're not calling it a problem. But you're also not fully okay leaving things exactly as they are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, I guess that's pretty much it. I still don't think I need like, treatment or whatever. But maybe I should... I don't know. Think about it a little. I'll think about it.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back, and I know last week was rough. Before we get into anything else — how are you doing right now, honestly?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here, right? Coach basically made it non-negotiable. It's not like I wanted to come back after last time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like you're being forced into this. Like the choice isn't really yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. And then I got that call about my labs on top of everything else. My mom's freaking out, Coach is on my case, and everyone's acting like I'm some kind of — I don't know, like I'm an alcoholic or something. I had a few beers at a party. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The lab results — what did the doctor actually tell you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My liver enzymes were, like, elevated. She said it was 'consistent with heavy alcohol use' or whatever. But I — look, I've been lifting hard, maybe it's from that. I literally read online that intense training can mess with those numbers.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've done some research, and part of you is hoping there's another explanation. And part of you maybe isn't so sure.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. It's just — this week was supposed to be better, right? I told myself I'd cut back, and then Thursday happened and... it just got out of hand. I didn't plan for it to go that way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you actually made a plan — you wanted to cut back — and then something happened Thursday that pulled you off course. Tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Guys on the team were going out after the scrimmage and I just... I didn't want to be the one sitting at home alone. That's how it always goes. I show up, I tell myself just two drinks, and then it's two in the morning and I don't even — I'm tired of it, honestly. I'm tired of feeling like garbage the next day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something to say. You set a limit for yourself, it didn't hold, and you're frustrated — not with me, not with Coach. With yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess so. It's like... I worked so hard to get here, you know? Scholarship, starting lineup sophomore year. And now I'm — I don't even know what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does football mean to you — like, underneath the scholarship, underneath what Coach thinks?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... it's everything. It's who I am. My dad played in college, my little brother looks up to me. When I'm on the field and everything's clicking it's the only time I don't feel like I'm in my head. It's the one place I actually feel like I know what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Football gives you clarity. Identity. A sense of being in control. And right now, the drinking is getting in the way of that — the thing that matters most to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yeah. I never really thought about it that way. I always thought going out with the guys was part of being on the team, like part of the brotherhood. But honestly? Half those guys aren't starting. I am. Or — I was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're starting to separate what actually serves you from what just feels like it does. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to lose my spot. I don't want my brother to come to a game and I'm sitting on the bench because I was out being an idiot. That's... that's not who I want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing. You came in frustrated, feeling pushed. But you also came in carrying something real — you made a plan last week, it didn't hold, and that bothered you. You're not okay with how things are. Football is your identity, your family is watching, and you said it clearly: this isn't who you want to be. So — what feels like a real first step, something you could actually do before we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not going out after scrimmages. Just for now. See if I can actually do it. And I should probably call the doctor back about the labs. I've been kind of ignoring that.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for coming in. I know you mentioned at the front desk you're squeezed for time between classes, so we'll work with whatever you've got. I'm Dr. Reeves. Make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I got like forty minutes maybe. I just — I saw the flyer in the student union and I don't even know why I came in, honestly. I'm probably fine. Like, I'm not the type of person who needs... this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something made you walk through that door though. What's been going on for you lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My friends did this whole... I don't know, they called it an intervention, which is — that's ridiculous. Like, we're in college. Everyone drinks on weekends. I had a couple rough nights, sure, but that's not a disorder or whatever. They're just being dramatic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your friends care enough to sit everyone down and say something — and your read on it is that they're overreacting. That what's been happening is just... normal college stuff.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean — okay, yeah, I blacked out a couple times this semester, but that happens to everyone. And I missed a lecture here and there because I was hungover, but my GPA is still fine. I'm not failing out. I honestly don't know what they want from me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When your friends sat you down for that conversation — what was that actually like for you in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Honestly? Embarrassing. Like, they were all sitting there looking at me like I was some kind of... I don't know. It felt like an ambush. My roommate was literally crying, which was weird. I mostly just wanted to leave. I kind of laughed it off but then that night I couldn't sleep, which — I mean, that's probably just stress from finals coming up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You laughed it off in the room, but then you couldn't sleep. And here you are. That tells me something about you — that even when something's uncomfortable, you don't just completely shut it out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess. Look, I'm not saying there's zero issue, I'm just saying it's not what they're making it out to be. I function. I go to class — mostly. I have a job lined up after graduation. It's not like I'm some — I'm not some alcoholic sitting under a bridge somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just make sure I'm following — there was an intervention, a sleepless night afterward, a job lined up, and you're mostly holding things together. That's a lot happening at once. Here's what I want to ask, and take your time with it: if drinking is doing exactly what you say — just normal stuff, no real cost — then what's been keeping you up at night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I don't know. Maybe... okay. There was this one night like three weeks ago where I woke up and I genuinely didn't know how I got home. And that was — that was kind of scary, actually. But it was one time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That scared you. Not knowing how you got home.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. My phone was dead and I had this bruise on my knee and I just — I had no memory of it. I remember sitting in my room thinking, okay, that was bad. But then the weekend came and I was out again so... I don't know what that says about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got this job lined up, you're almost at the finish line — senior year. What kind of person do you want to be walking into that next chapter?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone who has their stuff together. Like, I worked really hard to get here. Four years. I don't want to — I don't want to be the guy who blows it at the end. My dad never finished college, and I swore I'd be different, and I am. I just... I want to actually do something with it. Like actually make something of myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That means a lot to you — your dad's story, being different, making something real out of all of this. You've been carrying that for a long time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah. I don't really talk about that. But — look, I still don't think I'm like an addict or whatever. I'm not ready to say that. But I guess... maybe it wouldn't kill me to be more careful. On weekends. Or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in not totally sure why — but something pulled you here. Your friends reached out because they care, and even though that felt like an ambush, you couldn't shake it. There was a night that genuinely scared you. And underneath all of it, there's someone who wants to show up differently — for himself, for everything he's worked toward. You're not ready to put a label on anything, and that's completely okay. But that part of you that wants to make something of yourself? That part showed up today.

utterances.speaker: client
