utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. I still think my friends kind of overblew it, but — I don't know. Maybe I'll come back. I got class in ten minutes but... yeah. Maybe I'll come back.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know it can take a lot just to walk through that door the first time. So... what's brought you here? What's on your mind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... I guess my wife kind of pushed me to come. We've been having some arguments lately and she said she was worried about my drinking. I don't know, I figured it wouldn't hurt to talk to someone. I mean, I've been under a lot of stress with my PhD, so... I'm not opposed to being here or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your wife's concern brought you in, and there's a lot riding on you right now with the PhD. It sounds like part of you was open to coming — like you wanted to talk to someone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so. I mean, I don't think I have like a huge problem or anything, but... I've noticed I've been drinking more than I used to. Like it used to be a beer or two on weekends and now it's just — it's almost every night. I don't know when that shifted, honestly. It kind of snuck up on me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When did you notice that shift starting to happen?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably around... October? That's when my thesis proposal got pushed back and my advisor started giving me this look. I can't even describe it — it's just like, disappointment, I guess. And I'd come home and pour a glass of wine and it was just... it was the first moment all day where I could actually breathe. Like the noise in my head would just quiet down.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment of breathing — that relief — became really important to you. And your advisor... there's some pain there when you talk about him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, there is. I just — I don't feel like I belong there sometimes, you know? Like everyone else in my cohort just gets it and I'm sitting there Googling things I should already know. And then he told me my last chapter draft lacked rigor and I just... that one really hurt. I keep replaying it. Like, what if he's right? What if I'm not cut out for this?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's such a hard thing to sit with — questioning whether you belong, and then hearing something that seems to confirm that fear. How has all of this been affecting things at home, with your wife?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's been rough. She keeps saying I'm not present, that I come home and I'm just checked out. And I get defensive because she doesn't understand what this program is like, she doesn't get the pressure. But then last week she said if things don't change she's not sure she can stay, and I... I got really angry. And then I felt terrible. Like immediately after.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You got angry... and then terrible. Like the anger was covering something else underneath.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I was scared. I'm scared of losing her. And I'm scared that maybe she's right, and I don't want to admit that because then I have to actually deal with all of it. I'm just... I'm so tired. I'm tired of running from everything and I didn't even realize I was running until just now, saying that out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, and tell me if I'm getting it right. You came here partly because someone you love is worried — but also because some part of you has noticed this isn't working anymore. The drinking started as relief from feeling like you didn't belong, like your advisor was losing faith in you. And now it's creating distance with your wife, and you're exhausted from trying to hold all of it together alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. When you say it like that... it sounds worse than I let myself think about. I keep telling myself it's fine, it's temporary, it's just stress. But my grandfather was an alcoholic and I swore I'd never — I mean, I'm not that. But I can see how it starts. I can see the shape of it. And that... that actually scares me more than anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see the path it takes, and you don't want to walk down it. Can I ask — what drew you to the PhD in the first place? What does that work mean to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I actually love research. Like genuinely love it. I want to study how marginalized communities get misdiagnosed in healthcare, because my mom — she was misdiagnosed for years and it changed everything for our family. I want to be the person who helps fix that. That's why I'm doing this. And lately I haven't even been able to open my laptop without feeling like I'm going to fail before I even start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real why. Wanting to protect people like your mom, to do work that actually matters. That part of you — that's still in there. That hasn't gone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, it hasn't. I think I've just been... drowning, and I forgot why I jumped in. Does that make sense? I think I need to actually do something. Not just survive the week. Not just get to Friday so I can — yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're ready to do something — not just get through. What would feel like a real first step to you? Something doable, not overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe actually setting a limit — like a real one, not just telling myself 'just tonight' every night and then having three more. And maybe reaching out to the university counseling center. My advisor doesn't have to know. But I think I need more support than I've been letting myself have. I've been trying to do this alone and it's... clearly not working.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. ... I want you to know that means something. How have things been since we talked last week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... fine. It's been fine. I don't know why I'm back here, honestly. My boss basically said I had to, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you isn't sure this is worth your time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — look, I show up, I do my job. I've been bartending for four years. I know what I'm doing. The thing that happened, it was just... a one-off. People make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that — what happened, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I came in... I wasn't feeling great. Maybe I'd had a couple drinks before my shift. Like, to take the edge off, you know? And apparently I was — my manager said I was slurring. Which is ridiculous. I was tired. But nobody wants to hear that, so now I'm here talking to a therapist about my drinking like I'm some kind of... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels unfair. Like you got called out for something that felt completely normal to you — and now everyone's treating it as a big deal when you don't see it that way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And I just — yeah. ... I don't know. I mean, it's a bar. Everyone drinks. That's the culture. You can't work in a bar and be weird about alcohol, that's just... that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes a lot of sense given where you work. And... last time you said something that stayed with me. You said you couldn't remember the last day you didn't drink. I've been sitting with that. What does it feel like when you think about that now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Honestly? It's kind of messed up. Like, I went home after last session and I tried to actually think about it. When was the last time? And I — I genuinely couldn't land on a day. Not in like... months. Maybe longer.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That landed differently when you were alone with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah it did. I keep telling myself it's just — it's a wind-down thing. After a shift you need to decompress. But like... it's not just after shifts anymore. It's every day. It's mornings sometimes. And I don't... I don't really love admitting that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty to say. ... When you imagine a version of yourself that isn't doing this every day — what does that guy look like to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Like... clearer, maybe? I used to draw. Just for myself, nothing serious. I haven't done that in forever. I think when I drink I just kind of — zone out. Which is the point, right? But I don't actually do anything anymore. I just... exist at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You used to have a life after the shift. And somewhere along the way, the drinking kind of... replaced it. And you notice that. That's not a small thing to notice.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I think I've known for a while, honestly. I just didn't want to look at it. It's easier to say it's normal for bartenders, everyone does it, whatever. But maybe that's just something I tell myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I'm getting it right. You came in today feeling like this wasn't really your choice — your boss sent you here. And part of you still wanted to say the incident was a one-off, just the culture of the job. But when you actually sat with the question — when was the last sober day — you couldn't find one. And you're starting to wonder if the story you've been telling yourself, that this is just what bartenders do, is actually covering something else up. And there's a guy in there who used to draw. Who wants to be present for his own life.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. God, when you say it like that it sounds kind of bleak. But also like — I don't know. It doesn't feel hopeless, actually. That's weird. I kind of thought coming back here was going to feel worse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't have to feel hopeless. ... So — what would feel like a real first step? Not some big overhaul. Just something small. Something that feels like it belongs to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... trying one night. Like, after a shift, just one night where I don't. See what it actually feels like. I don't know if I can do it but — I think I want to try.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this wasn't exactly your idea — from what I understand, your family was pretty insistent. So, what's your sense of why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my mom basically dragged me here. I had a DUI a couple weeks ago and everyone's acting like I'm some kind of alcoholic or something. I'm not. It was one bad night, I just — I made a mistake. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So in your mind, this is one isolated incident — not something that points to a bigger pattern.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, I work in marketing, I go to events, I network — it's literally part of my job. Everyone drinks at these things. I just... I drove when I shouldn't have. It happens. I'm not proud of it but it doesn't make me an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned it's part of the job — the events, the networking. What does a typical week actually look like for you, in terms of drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, like... normal? A few nights a week, maybe more on weekends if there's something going on. That's just what people in my industry do. I'm not sitting home alone polishing off a bottle every night, so — I mean, why is that even the question here?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A few nights a week, more on weekends — and at the same time, you ended up with a DUI. Part of you is saying this is totally normal, just how it works in your world. And I wonder if another part of you is sitting with something else about that night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — okay, yeah, obviously I feel terrible. Like, what if I had actually hurt someone? I've thought about that. I have. But that doesn't mean I have a drinking problem. It means I had bad judgment one night. Those are two completely different things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today, even though you really didn't want to. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I just... I don't want my family thinking I'm some mess. I'm not. I have a good job, I have my own apartment, I'm doing fine. I just — I don't want this one thing to blow everything up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Having your life together — the job, the independence — what does that mean to you? What's important about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything. I watched my parents struggle my whole childhood and I swore I wasn't gonna end up like that. I'm 28, I worked really hard to get here. I just... I don't want this to be the thing that defines me. You know? Like, that's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something you're genuinely proud of. And the DUI feels like a threat to that — to how you see yourself, and how other people see you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And like... okay, honestly? Sometimes I get home after these events and I just feel so exhausted and kind of... hollow? And I pour a glass of wine and it's like, okay, I can finally breathe. I don't know if that's — I don't know what that is, I've never really said that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, because there's a lot here. You've worked incredibly hard. You're proud of what you've built and you don't see yourself as someone with a drinking problem — and at the same time, the DUI happened. And just now you described something where alcohol is doing a specific job for you — helping you decompress, manage that hollow feeling after a long day. You haven't really examined why until right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... I don't know. I haven't let myself think about it that way. I just kind of do it and move on. That's probably not — yeah. That's probably not great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not a question you've let yourself sit with until now. So let me ask — not what your mom wants, not what the court ordered — what do you want? If you imagine yourself six months from now, what would feel different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I just... I want to stop feeling like I'm running all the time. Like, I'd actually like to go home after a long week and just be okay. Not need something to wind down. I don't even know if that's possible for me at this point but... yeah. That actually sounds kind of nice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just named something real. You want to actually rest — not just get through the night. And you can picture what that might feel like, even if you're not sure how to get there yet. That's an honest place to be starting from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm still not like, convinced I'm an alcoholic or whatever. But I guess I'm willing to figure out what's actually going on. Maybe. That's more than I thought I'd be saying when I walked in here, so.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, good to see you again. Come on in, make yourself comfortable. How have things been going since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... fine, I guess. Same as always. I don't really know why I keep coming here, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not sure this is worth your time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like, no offense, but my school counselor basically pushed me into this and everyone's acting like I'm some kind of problem when I'm literally just — I don't know. It was one party. Everyone was drinking. I'm not the only one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds really unfair — like you got singled out for something you see everyone around you doing. I did want to check in though, because last time things felt like they were going okay, and today feels different. What happened this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... um... okay so there was this thing last weekend. With my friends. And I know what you're gonna say, but it kind of got out of hand and I... I woke up and I didn't really remember getting home. And my mom found out and now she's watching me like every second and it's just — it's so suffocating.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not remembering how you got home. That sounds really unsettling.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I wasn't scared at the time. But like, after — yeah, I guess it was kind of... weird. I don't like not knowing what happened. I texted my friend and she filled me in and it wasn't like, anything bad happened. But still.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You value knowing what's happening around you — being aware, being safe. That clearly matters to you. What was going through your mind when you realized the pieces weren't there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just kept thinking like — what if something did happen, you know? And that's not... that's not me. Like I'm usually the responsible one in my friend group. I'm the one making sure everyone else is okay. And that night I couldn't even... I couldn't even account for myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The person your friends count on. And this time you couldn't be that person — not even for yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I keep telling myself it's not a big deal, but... my mom wasn't even yelling, which is almost worse? She was just really quiet. Really disappointed. And I just... I hate that. I hate being the reason she looks like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you is starting to wonder if this is turning into something different than just hanging out and having fun. What do you think is driving it lately — like underneath all of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I think... okay, this whole year has just been a lot. College apps, figuring out what I'm even doing with my life. I got into a school but I'm not sure it's the right one, and everyone around me has this whole plan and I'm just kind of... floating. And drinking is like the only time I actually stop thinking. It just — it shuts everything off for a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gives you a break from all that noise. And that makes complete sense — you've been carrying a lot this year. That same thing is also what's starting to worry you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess it is. Like I'm not stupid — I know that's not... using something to cope like that, that's a red flag, right? That's what they always say. And I used to roll my eyes at that stuff but now I'm sitting here and I'm like... am I that person?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know your own patterns better than you give yourself credit for. So let me ask you something — forget what your mom wants, forget what school expects. When you picture the next few months, getting through this transition, what do you actually want it to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I just... I want to feel okay without needing something to make me feel okay. Like I want to be able to go to a party and have one drink and just — be fine. Not need to keep going until everything's off. I don't know if I can do that but... that's what I'd want. I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing today. You came in feeling like you'd gone backwards. But you had a night that genuinely shook you, and instead of brushing it off entirely, you're here asking hard questions — about why it's happening, about what you want your life to actually look like. That takes something. That's a real shift from where you were a few weeks ago. So what feels like one thing you could do before we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... actually talk to my mom. Not wait for her to stop being disappointed, but like, actually say something. And maybe start figuring out the school thing for real, because I think a lot of this is coming from me just not knowing what I'm doing. I'm still kind of scared but... I don't know. It doesn't feel totally hopeless today.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you. So we're — what is this, session five? Six? Before we dive into anything, I just want to do a quick check-in. How are you walking in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: How am I walking in. You really asking me that? I'm walking in because if I don't show up here I violate my probation, that's how I'm walking in. I don't wanna be here. Wasn't happy about it the first time, I'm not happy about it now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It still feels like something being done to you, not something you chose.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because it IS something being done to me. And now on top of all that, my boss pulls me aside Tuesday, says he 'heard some things' about why I missed those days. And Marcus's school calls — his counselor says he's acting out in class. So I got all of that going on and I gotta come sit here and... I don't even know what we're supposed to be doing here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a lot coming at you from different directions all at once — your job, what's happening with Marcus, the court requirements. With all of that in the room right now, what feels most urgent to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — Marcus. Obviously Marcus. But I don't see what me being here has to do with any of that. I'm not — look, I made some bad calls, okay? I know that. But they're treating me like I can't take care of my own kid. Like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It's just not fair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's this sense of being judged — like people have already decided who you are. And even in the middle of all that anger, you keep coming back to Marcus.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I do. Because he's eight years old, he doesn't understand why dad's always stressed out or... I don't know if he knows about the DUI stuff. God, I hope he doesn't. But kids pick up on things, right? Like even if you don't say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that you're thinking about what Marcus is picking up on — what he's experiencing — that tells me something about you as a father. That matters to you deeply.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Of course it matters. He's my kid. I'm not gonna... look, I'm not gonna pretend I've been perfect. I know I haven't. But I do care about him. It's just everything kind of — I don't know, this past week especially just felt like too much all at once.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned the last couple weeks had actually been going okay, and then this week felt like too much. What happened that threw things off?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. The last couple weeks were — I mean, they were okay. I wasn't drinking. I was showing up to stuff. And then Tuesday happened with my boss and I just... I had a couple beers that night. I'm not proud of it. It wasn't like before but it happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm tracking everything. You came in today feeling forced into this, frustrated, a lot hitting you from all sides — your job, Marcus, the court. But you also just told me that before this week, things were actually going okay. You weren't drinking, you were showing up. Then a really hard moment hit on Tuesday and you had a couple beers, and you're not proud of that. That's a lot of ground to be holding.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. I mean I'm not proud of Tuesday. But it wasn't a blackout thing. I had two beers, I went to bed. I didn't drive anywhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You made a deliberate choice not to drive. Even when things were spiraling, that line held.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well. Yeah. I mean I'm not stupid. I learned that lesson. Hard way, twice, but I learned it. I just — I didn't call anybody. I probably should've but I... I just sat with it instead.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would calling someone have looked like in that moment? What got in the way?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Pride, probably. I hate asking for help. Always have. It feels like — like admitting I can't handle my own stuff. Which is dumb, I know it's dumb when I actually say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes complete sense that you've been doing this alone — that's been your way of getting through things for a long time. And what I'm hearing today, underneath all the frustration you walked in with, is someone who genuinely wants to be there for Marcus, who knows when something didn't go right, and who's starting to ask himself harder questions out loud. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I just want things to be okay. For him, mostly. But also just — for me too. I'm tired. I'm tired of being angry all the time.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. I imagine it probably took a lot to walk through that door. What feels most important for you to talk about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my advisor basically said I had to. I got a DUI a few weeks ago but it's — look, it was one night. I'd had a really bad week at work and I just wasn't thinking. I don't usually drive after drinking. It was a mistake, okay? One mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this really doesn't feel like you — like it was out of character for who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, I'm not — I'm not an alcoholic or whatever. I go to happy hours, yeah, but everyone in marketing does. It's basically part of the job. I just want to put this behind me and move on with my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to put it behind you. And at the same time... you just went through a detox program. That's not a small thing. What was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... humiliating, honestly. I kept thinking — I have a good job, I worked hard, I shouldn't be there. But then there were these moments at like three in the morning where I just couldn't stop crying and I didn't even know why. That... that scared me a little, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about those nights got to you in a way you weren't expecting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, a little. But it's not like — I've been under so much stress, okay? My boss is constantly on my case, I've been trying to hit these targets, and drinking helps me decompress after. That's not the same as having a problem. Tons of people do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot right now — work pressure, this whole situation, worrying about what people think. When you step back from all of that... what matters most to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My career. My reputation. I've worked really hard to get where I am and if people at work found out about this... God. That's what keeps me up at night. I don't want to be seen as someone who can't handle her own life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your career, your reputation — those mean everything to you. And there's a part of you that's afraid what's been happening might be putting those very things at risk.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I hate that you said that because it's true. I keep telling myself it's fine but my supervisor has made comments — little things. About me seeming distracted, coming in late. I didn't think anyone noticed. But I guess they did.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real courage to say that out loud. You've been carrying all of this alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I have. My friends think it's just like... oh, Maya had a wild night. They don't get it. And I can't tell my mom because she would completely spiral. So I've just been sitting with it, trying to figure out if I'm okay or if I'm... not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm hearing you right. You came in today feeling like this was just one mistake to get through. And yet — there were those nights in detox that shook you, your supervisor has been noticing things, and you've been sitting alone with all of this, asking yourself whether you're really okay. That's a lot to hold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...When you say it like that it sounds like more than I wanted it to be. I think I've been really good at convincing myself everything's fine. I'm good at that. Convincing people.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm curious — if this weight wasn't on you anymore, if things were actually different... what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'd feel more like myself. I used to feel sharp at work, like I was on top of everything. Now I just feel like I'm holding it together with tape. I don't want to feel like that anymore. I want to actually feel okay. Not just look okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want something real — not just the appearance of being fine, but actually feeling it. That part of you that knows something could be different? That part matters a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I'm still not ready to say I have a problem problem, you know? But I think I'm willing to... look at it. Actually look at it this time. That's something, right?

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not going to pretend this is where you wanted to be today. You were mandated here, so let's just be straight about that. I'm not here to lecture you or run back to your parents with everything you say. So — what's your take on why you're sitting in that chair right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because my parents freaked out. Over literally nothing. They found some bottles in my room and now it's like... I don't know, end of the world or whatever. So here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Over nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah. It's not like I'm some... I don't know. Everyone drinks. It's not a big deal. They're making it into this whole thing and it's like, relax.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would you want me to know about you that I'm probably not going to find in that court paperwork?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I'm not like... some addict or whatever they think I am. I'm a normal kid. I get decent grades. I'm not out here destroying my life. It was one night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're sixteen, you're sitting in a counselor's office you didn't ask to be in, and everyone around you is treating you like a problem that needs fixing. That's exhausting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. Exactly. Nobody actually asked me anything. They just decided.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about the night that ended up here. What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was stupid. There was a party, I had some drinks — like, a lot, okay, fine — and I got in a car with this guy who I thought was okay to drive and he wasn't and... we got pulled over. That's it. It was one bad call.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And since then — what's it been like at home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My dad doesn't talk to me. Like at all. My mom cries whenever I walk into the room and I don't know what to do with that. It's like... I didn't kill anyone. I just — I made a mistake and now it's like I don't even exist in my own house.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is still angry that everyone overreacted — and at the same time, something about watching your mom cry and your dad go silent... that's getting to you too. Both of those things can be true.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know. Maybe. I didn't really think I was scaring them. I just — that night I just wanted to not think for a while. Like everything gets so loud and when I'm drinking it just... goes quiet. You know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Everything gets loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like... school stuff, my parents were already fighting a lot before all this, I just — I don't know how to explain it. It's easier to just not feel it. And I know that sounds bad when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty — most people your age in this room just keep saying they don't have a problem and run out the clock. The fact that you can actually name what it does for you, that you're using it to turn the volume down on something that's too loud? That's not nothing. That's you knowing yourself. So I want to ask you something straight — what do you think happens when that quiet gets harder and harder to find without it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I haven't thought about it like that. That's kind of... I don't know, that's a little scary actually. Because it's already like — it takes more than it used to. To feel the same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you walked in here ready to do your hour and get out. And somewhere in here you told me about things being loud, about your dad not talking to you, about needing more to feel the same — things I'm guessing you haven't said to anybody. That's where the real work is, if you want it. Not checking a box. What would it mean to you to actually figure out what's underneath all this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe... maybe it'd actually help? Like I'm so tired of everything feeling like this. I've never talked to anyone about any of this before so I don't really know how it works but... yeah. Maybe.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — I'm glad you made it. I know you mentioned you're pressed for time, so no pressure at all. Just... wherever you want to start is fine.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I don't really know why I'm here, honestly. I saw something online and I had like twenty minutes between classes so I figured whatever. It's probably nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something drew you in, even with everything you had going on today. What was it about what you saw that made you think, even just for a second, it might be worth stopping by?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was about drinking, I think. And like, depression or whatever. And I just — look, I'm not some alcoholic, okay? I drink like a normal person. I've just been having a rough couple months and it's been a little more than usual. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So things have been harder lately, and the drinking has kind of crept up alongside that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — yeah. The depression stuff, that's been going on a while. I got diagnosed like... three years ago? I was in therapy for a bit but it didn't really go anywhere so I stopped. I just kind of deal with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying a lot on your own for a while. What does 'dealing with it' actually look like for you, on a hard day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I come home, I have a few drinks, watch something, go to bed. That's the routine. And I already know what you're gonna say, okay? I've heard the whole speech. The last therapist I had spent half our sessions telling me what I should and shouldn't be doing, like I'm some kind of child, and I just — I'm not doing that again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds exhausting — feeling like you were being told what to do instead of actually listened to. And yet you still came back and tried again today. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I guess. I don't know. My girlfriend kind of mentioned it too, so. It wasn't just me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So someone close to you noticed too. It sounds like there are people in your life who care about what's going on with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's frustrated with me. I get it. I get frustrated with me too, honestly. Like, I know a few drinks every night isn't exactly — I'm not stupid. But it's the only thing that actually takes the edge off. The depression is just so... heavy sometimes. And I don't know what else to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's doing something real for you in those moments — giving you actual relief from something that's genuinely heavy. If you imagine a version of your life where you didn't need it for that... what would have to be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. That's a weird question. I guess I'd have to actually feel okay without it. Like, not just numb, but actually okay. Which I honestly can't picture right now. I haven't felt that way in a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So what I'm hearing is — you've got the depression that's been weighing on you for years, the drinking that fills a gap but also adds its own weight, a relationship that's feeling the strain, and a history of feeling like therapy just wasn't for you. And yet here you are. Something in you hasn't quite given up on things being different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that it sounds... a lot. It is a lot. I think I've just been telling myself it's fine because otherwise I'd actually have to deal with it, and that's — honestly that's the scarier option.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real courage to sit with that — to say out loud, 'maybe it's not fine.' That is not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, maybe. I think I just — I actually want to feel better. Like genuinely better, not just less bad. I don't know if that's possible, but I want to find out. Maybe. As long as this doesn't turn into another lecture situation.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No lectures. I promise. Just us figuring it out together, at whatever pace actually works for you. You walked in here today — that already tells me something about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. Okay yeah. I can — I think I can do that. Can we set up an actual appointment? Like not just walking in next time?

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. And I want to say — you came back. A lot of people don't make it to a second session, so that tells me something about you. [pause] How are you doing today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I... I almost didn't. I sat in my car for like twenty minutes before I came in. [pause] Not great, honestly. Not great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty minutes in the car. Something made you walk through that door though. What was going through your mind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. My — ex-wife, she keeps texting me. Saying I need to do something about myself. And I'm like, what do you want from me at this point, you know? But also... I've been drinking more than I should. Even I can see that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a lot in that. She's pushing, and part of you is frustrated by that... and yet there's also this other part that's noticing something that concerns you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, look — I'm not some alcoholic sitting on a park bench, okay? I go to work every day. I function. It's just... since everything happened... [exhales] The nights are long. You come home to an empty house and there's just... nothing there. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The house is empty now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My kids used to — I'd come home and they'd be loud, fighting over the TV, and I'd be like, 'guys, give me five minutes.' [voice breaks] And now I would give anything for that. I'd give anything. I don't... I don't know how to do this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't just lose the marriage. You lost the whole life — the noise, the chaos, even the parts that drove you crazy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sandra always said I was never present. Always at work, always on my phone. And maybe... maybe she was right, I don't know. And now I'm sitting there drinking bourbon watching sports I don't even care about thinking — this is what I traded it for? This?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a hard thing to sit with — that kind of recognition. What do you miss most? If you could just... have one piece of it back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter. She's eleven. She called me last week and we talked for like three minutes and then she had to go to soccer and I just... I sat there with the phone in my hand for I don't know how long. [clears throat] She needs her dad to be okay. I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She called you. And you picked up. You're still her dad — that hasn't changed, even when everything else has.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I don't want her to see me like this. My dad was a drinker and I swore I'd never — [stops himself] I don't want to be that guy. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came back today even when it was hard. You can see the drinking has gone somewhere you didn't intend. You're carrying a lot of grief — for the marriage, for the family life you had, for the kind of father you wanted to be. And underneath all of that, there's this very strong pull toward your daughter. This belief that she still needs you, and that you can still show up for her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... [long exhale] I don't want to waste this. Whatever's left. I don't want to waste it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would not wasting it look like for you? What's one thing that feels possible right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... actually cutting back. Not just saying it, actually doing it. And calling her more. She'd like that. I think she'd like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today not sure you wanted to be here. And now you're talking about calling your daughter more, about actually making a change — not because someone's forcing you, but because of what you care about. That's yours. That came from you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quiet] Yeah, I think it is.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this wasn't exactly your idea, so I appreciate you making the time. Before we get into anything, I just want to hear from you — what's your take on why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My doctor told me I had to come. Said my liver numbers were... I don't know, off or whatever. I think he's making a bigger deal out of it than it is. I feel fine. I've been doing this job for twenty years, I'm not some — I'm not an alcoholic or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you showed up even though you're not sure any of this is necessary. That tells me something about you — you take your health seriously enough to at least hear people out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I guess. Look, I'm not trying to be difficult. I just — the guy barely looked at me for ten minutes and now I'm sitting in a therapy office. No offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: None taken. It makes sense you'd feel brushed off — referral comes out of nowhere, now you're here. What do you actually know about what showed up on those tests?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He said my... enzymes. Liver enzymes were elevated. ALT something. I looked it up after and it said that can happen from, like, a bad week. Stress. Ibuprofen. I take a lot of ibuprofen for my knees. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You did your homework. And yeah, ibuprofen can do it. So can alcohol, over time. You mentioned drinking — what does a typical week look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Six beers at night. After work. I'm in construction — you know what that does to your body? I come home, I eat, I have my beers, I watch TV, I go to bed. It's not... it's a routine. That's it. Guys I work with drink way more than me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Six beers every night — that's how you decompress after a brutal day on the job. And you're comparing yourself to the guys around you and thinking, I'm not the worst one. I get that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. I'm not... I don't drink at work. I don't drive drunk. I handle my business. So why is everyone acting like I got a problem?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got clear lines you don't cross. That matters to you — being responsible. I want to ask you something and I'd like you to just sit with it for a second. When the doctor showed you those numbers... what went through your head? Not what you told him. What you actually felt.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... um. I don't know. I was — look, I got a daughter. She's sixteen. And for a second I thought... I thought about my dad. He died at fifty-one. Heart stuff. And I was like, what if this is that. What if this is how it starts. But then I looked it up and it said—

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You thought about your daughter. And your dad.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't — I'm not trying to go out at fifty-one. He never... he never saw me do anything, you know? I don't want that for her. I don't want her to be sitting somewhere at thirty saying her dad wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I share something with you? Just so you have the full picture — and then you can do whatever you want with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Six beers a night is about forty-two a week. That's well into the range where the liver starts to accumulate damage — quietly, without symptoms, for years. By the time you feel it, it's usually already significant. The elevated enzymes your doctor saw are the liver saying hey, something's happening. That's not nothing. And it's also not a death sentence — not if you catch it now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I didn't know it added up like that. Forty-two. I never — when you put a number on it like that it sounds... I don't know. That's a lot. I just. It doesn't feel like that much when it's just, like, end of the day, six beers.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing. You came in ready to push back, and honestly you had reasons to. But somewhere in this conversation you mentioned your dad, your daughter, and the fact that this number scared you more than you let on to your doctor. That's not a guy who doesn't care. That's a guy who cares a lot and hasn't had a reason to stop yet. So — what would it mean to you if you actually made a change here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... I'd be around. Like, actually around. Not just alive but — present, I guess. I don't know if I can do it cold but I'm not saying no. I'm just saying I never really thought about stopping before. Maybe I should start thinking about it.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. So last time you were feeling like things were starting to click a little more — how have the past couple weeks been for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... okay, I guess? Like, there were some good days. I had a few days where I didn't drink at all, which felt... I don't know, different. Good different. But then last weekend kind of fell apart so. I don't want to make it a big thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A few days without drinking — that's actually not a small thing, even if it doesn't feel that way right now. And something happened last weekend that made it harder.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was my cousin's birthday back home. They did a video call and everyone was there, my whole family, and I'm just... sitting in my apartment alone watching them through a screen. And after I hung up I just — I didn't even think about it, I just opened a bottle. It's not like I planned it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment of hanging up and the apartment going quiet — what was that like for you, in your body, right before you reached for it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe it. Like a... a weight? No, more like a hollow feeling. And I know you're going to say I should have called someone or gone for a walk or whatever but you don't understand — there's nobody to call here. I don't have people here. That's the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not wrong. I'm not going to pretend that "just call a friend" is an answer when the whole reason this is so hard is that you're building from zero in a place where you don't have that yet. That hollow feeling makes complete sense.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. Sorry, I just — people keep acting like it's a willpower thing and it makes me want to scream. My sister thinks I just need to "put myself out there" more. She has no idea. She's never had to start over somewhere where she doesn't even understand half the jokes people make.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds exhausting — feeling misunderstood even by people who love you. What do you wish they understood?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I'm... I'm trying. I really am. I came here because I wanted a better life and now I'm here and it's like — what was the point? I'm lonelier than I've ever been. And the drinking, it's the only time I feel like I can just... stop. Stop trying so hard just to exist.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying something really heavy. And somewhere underneath all of this — you still want the life you came here for. That hasn't gone away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I think so. I don't know. Some days I'm not sure anymore. Like last weekend felt like going backwards. And I'd had, what, five or six good days? And then one phone call and I just erased all of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One hard night doesn't erase five good days — those days happened. They're yours. But I want to ask you something, and take your time with it — when you imagine this getting better, what does that actually look like for you? Not the drinking specifically, but your life here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think about having... like, one person. Just one person who I could text and say "I'm having a rough night" and they'd get it. That's all I want, honestly. I don't need a big group or anything. Just one person who's actually here, not six time zones away.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One real connection. Someone present. And you can picture that — you know exactly what it would feel like to have it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I can. There's actually this woman at my job — we've had lunch twice. She's from the Philippines, she's been here longer than me. She kind of gets the adjustment thing. I've been kind of... holding back? I don't know why. Maybe I'm scared she'll think I'm too much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing — you came in today a little deflated after a hard weekend, and you've been sitting with this feeling that you erased your progress. But what I'm also hearing is: you had nearly a week of real change, you know exactly what you're looking for in terms of connection, and there's actually someone already in your life who might be part of that picture. That's not someone going backwards. That's someone who knows a lot about themselves.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... I don't know, it sounds less bleak. I think I've been so focused on the one bad night that I forgot about the other days. And yeah. Maybe I should ask her if she wants to get coffee sometime. Outside of work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took guts to even consider, especially when you've been protecting yourself. What feels possible between now and next time we meet?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I can ask her. And maybe — next time I'm on a call with my family and it starts to feel like that, I can try to text her instead of just sitting there with the feeling. I'm not saying I'll be perfect. But... I want to try. I actually want to try.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you came back. I'm glad you're here. Last time we ended on kind of a heavy note — how's this week been for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's been whatever. My sister's still being dramatic about everything, so that's fun. I had a few events this week though, which was nice. Got some really great content actually. People loved my Cabo throwback series — like, the engagement was insane.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sounds like you've been keeping busy. And yet... there's something about how you said 'whatever' that makes me wonder if it's been heavier than the highlight reel.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Brianna's birthday was Tuesday. She didn't invite me. We've been friends for six years and I found out through Instagram — through a tagged photo, like I'm some random person. Which is, like, beyond mortifying. But whatever, she's been doing this whole wellness era thing lately so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Six years. Finding out through a photo. What was going through your head when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I laughed it off at first, obviously. Like there had to be a mistake, right? So I texted her and she left me on read for three days. Three days. And I know why. She thinks I'm a bad influence now. Which is insane — I'm literally one of her oldest friends. But I guess marrying some guy from Connecticut and going sober makes you too good for your actual friends.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being shut out by someone who's known you that long — that's a real loss. And it sounds like it's not the first time lately you've felt people pulling away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. People leave. My ex left, my mom's basically checked out since the holidays, now Brianna... I'm starting to think maybe I'm just — I don't know. Too much. Or not enough. I genuinely can't tell anymore which one it is. Both? Neither? I literally don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Too much and not enough at the same time. Like you can't quite find solid ground with who you are to the people around you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I had like four drinks before this session, by the way. Just so you know. It was brunch, it was a completely normal Sunday thing, and I'm not hiding it. I just wanted to say it before you asked or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you telling me that. That actually takes something — to just put it on the table. What made you want to mention it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because everyone's making it into this massive thing and it wasn't. It was brunch. Normal people drink at brunch. I just wanted to get ahead of it before you turned it into a whole moment. And now I'm annoyed I even brought it up because now it's a thing. See? This is what I mean. I can't win.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You got ahead of it. You named it yourself, before I could. What do you think that's about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. Maybe because it's been louder lately. Like, not louder in a bad way, it's just — there's more of it. The drinking. And I notice it. I notice it and then I notice that I'm noticing it, and then I just... pour another one anyway. Which is fine. It's fine, I just — I don't know why I said that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're watching yourself. Some part of you is paying very close attention, even when the other part keeps going.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Awareness doesn't really fix anything, does it. Like I'm fully aware that my sister dragged me here, that Brianna's ghosting me, that I had drinks before a ten AM session. Being aware just makes it louder. Congrats, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Awareness makes it louder. And yet here you are. You came back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. My sister gets off my back for a week if I show up, so there's that. But also — I guess some part of me is just tired. Not of drinking, that's not what I'm saying. But of how hard I'm working to make everything look okay. It's a lot. It's a lot of work and I'm really tired.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just try to hold some of this for a second. You lost a friend this week — or it feels that way. Your sister pushed you here, but some part of you came anyway. You're noticing the drinking more than you used to, and underneath all the events and the content and the brunch, there's this exhaustion — of working really hard to make everything look fine when it doesn't feel fine.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's — I hate that that's accurate. But yeah. That's pretty much it.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, make yourself comfortable. There's no rush at all. I'm glad you came in today — can you tell me a little bit about what brought you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, uh... honestly I'm not really sure what I'm supposed to be doing here. My doctor, she kind of... she suggested I come. Said there were some numbers on my bloodwork she didn't like. Something about my liver. I don't know, I figured I'd see what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your doctor flagged something, and that was enough to get you through the door — even if you're not quite sure what to expect from being here. That takes something, just showing up when you don't know what you're walking into.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess. I mean... she mentioned my drinking. Which, look, I've been retired for about three years now and I do have a drink or two in the evenings, sometimes more. But I don't think it's — I mean, it's not like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It's not that serious.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A drink in the evenings, sometimes more. And part of you is saying it's probably not a big deal... and yet here you are. I'm wondering what it's been like, these three years since you retired.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's been... harder than I expected. I thought retirement was supposed to be the good part, you know? Thirty-eight years working for the county, and I just — I thought I'd be relieved. But it's quiet. Real quiet. My wife passed four years ago, so it's just me in the house and... I don't know. The days are long.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The quiet got louder than you expected. Thirty-eight years of purpose, of structure, of being somewhere you were needed — and then just... silence. And your wife not being there either.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I used to have somewhere to be every morning. People who needed things from me. Now I wake up and there's just... coffee and the news. Sometimes I don't talk to another person for two, three days at a stretch. My kids are busy, they've got their own lives. I don't want to be a burden. So I just... I keep to myself mostly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot of that alone, trying not to be a burden to the people you love. I want to ask you something gently — when you pour that drink in the evening, what does it do for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... takes the edge off, I suppose. Makes the evening feel less empty. I'll put on the TV and have a few and it's like — the loneliness isn't quite so loud. I know that probably sounds... I don't know. Sad. When I say it out loud it sounds sad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound sad to me — it sounds human. You found something that gives you a little relief from a very real pain. And it sounds like part of you is starting to wonder whether that relief might be costing you something too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... when she showed me those numbers. The liver enzymes or whatever. She had this look on her face, my doctor. She's known me for fifteen years and she just... I could tell she was worried. And I thought, okay, maybe I've let this get a little out of hand. Maybe more than a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted when you saw her face. What is it that you'd want to protect — if you think about what really matters to you, what comes to mind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My grandkids. I've got three of them, youngest is five. I want to... I want to see them grow up, you know? I want to be there for that. And I don't want them to remember their grandpa as somebody who just... sat in a dark house and drank himself into the ground. That's not — that's not the man I want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That matters deeply to you — being present for them, being the grandfather you want to be. That's not a small thing. That's who you are at your core.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I've been grieving. My wife, my career, my whole — the whole life I had. And I just didn't know what to do with all of it so I drank instead of dealing with it. I can see that now. I don't know why I can see it now and not six months ago, but I can.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see it now, and that's what's here in this moment. If you think about taking one small step — just one — what feels like it might be possible?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I don't know, maybe talking to someone. Like this, but more regularly. And there's a senior center about two miles from my house. I drove past it a hundred times but I never went in. Maybe I could try that. Something. Anything that isn't just sitting there waiting for the day to end.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing from you today, because I think it's worth pausing on. You came in not knowing what to expect, carrying a lot of loss — your wife, your work, the structure that gave your days meaning. You found something that quieted that pain for a while. And today, you connected what you really want — to be there for your grandchildren, to be the man you know yourself to be — with a real willingness to try something different. That's not a small thing. That's the beginning of something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think it might be. I came in here thinking I was just going to get a pamphlet or something. I didn't expect to... feel like maybe there's actually something I can do about all this. I'm not saying it'll be easy. But I think I'm ready to try.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today... especially after everything that happened this week. How are you feeling right now, just sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm fine. Honestly the whole ER thing was way overblown. My roommate panicked and called 911 like I was actually dying or something. I just had a rough night. It happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. Your roommate was scared for you, and that felt like too much.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, because it was. I know my limits, I've been doing this for years. I'm an artist - like, this is just how it works. You drink, you feel things, you make things. Van Gogh wasn't exactly sober, you know? Nobody talks about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking has been part of your creative identity for a long time. I'm curious... how has the work actually been lately? What's been coming out of the studio?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Don't. Okay? Don't do that thing where you... ugh. It's been a hard month. A hard few months. I've been blocked, which is why I've been drinking more - to try to get through it. That's not some big revelation, that's just how creative blocks work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds exhausting. Reaching for something to break through, and still feeling stuck. You're fighting hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. It's supposed to work. Or... I don't know. Lately I'll sit down at the canvas and I've had a couple glasses and I just - I paint garbage. Total garbage. And then I drink more because I painted garbage and then it gets worse and I just... God, I don't even know why I'm saying that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about saying that out loud feels important. What's it like, noticing that pattern?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... kind of terrifying, actually. Like. If the thing I thought was helping isn't actually helping then... what? What am I without that story? I've told myself this for ten years. That I need it to feel anything worth painting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The story you've held onto - that alcohol opens something up in you - and now you're starting to wonder if maybe it's been... closing things down instead.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I look at stuff I made five, six years ago and it's so much better. And I was drinking then but not... not like this. Not every single day just to feel normal. I used to actually feel things sober. Raw things. When did that stop? I don't even know when that stopped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a difference you're starting to see - between drinking that once felt like freedom, and this, which sounds more like... needing it just to get to zero. Just to feel okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. Yeah, that's actually - that's a really good way to put it. I don't even get that loose, inspired feeling anymore. I just feel less bad. That's not the same thing, is it. That's not creativity, that's just... maintenance.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It really isn't the same. I'm wondering... who was that artist, five or six years ago? What did making work feel like before it got to this point?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She was... God. She was kind of fearless, actually. I'd just go in and experiment and not care if it was good. Now every piece feels like it has to prove something. Like I have to justify being here, taking up space. The drinking was supposed to quiet that voice but it just... it got louder. It got so much louder.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You came in today after a really frightening night. You've carried this belief for years that drinking is woven into who you are as an artist - and it was true for you once, it did open something. And now you're sitting with this uncomfortable possibility that somewhere along the way, it stopped being that. The art has gotten harder. The freedom has been replaced by just needing to feel okay. And the fearless version of you feels very far away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...when you say it like that I want to cry. Yeah. That's it. That's exactly it. I miss her. I actually miss myself and I didn't even let myself think that until just now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's still there. I really believe that. And I want to ask you - with everything you've just said... what feels even a little bit possible to you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I can do like, cold turkey or whatever. That scares me. But... maybe I could try one morning. Sober. Just me and the canvas, see what happens. I haven't done that in... I genuinely cannot remember the last time I did that.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hello, Mrs. Callahan. I'm glad you came in today. I know you were just discharged yesterday — that couldn't have been easy. There's no agenda here, no rush. I'd just like to understand a little bit about what's been going on for you lately, if that's alright.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... my daughter basically dragged me here. I told her I was fine. I don't really see what talking is gonna do, but... here I am, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because of the pressure from your family — not necessarily because you felt like you needed to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah, that's about right. She worries too much. Always has.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me a little about what the last few months have looked like for you — the pain, the hospital visit, all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've had this back pain for — God, must be three years now. The doctors give me pills but they don't... they don't always touch it. So I have a glass of wine at night, maybe two, just to take the edge off. It helps me sleep. I don't think that's... I mean, plenty of people do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The medication alone isn't enough, and the wine helps fill in the gaps — gets you through the night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. It's not like I'm — I'm not some kind of alcoholic sitting in a bar all day. I'm just trying to manage. I'm seventy-two years old, I think I've earned a little peace at night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And then something happened that landed you in the ER. What was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That was... that scared me, I'll admit it. I don't remember calling 911. My daughter found me on the floor. I... I don't know exactly what I took or how much, I just — that part is gone. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real courage to say that out loud, especially when it's that frightening. You didn't have to come today. But you did.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just — I don't want to scare her again. That's the only reason. I don't want to be a burden. She has her own family, her own problems, she doesn't need to be up at three in the morning worrying about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not wanting to be a burden — that's a very deep part of who you are. And yet, even with all that effort to protect her... she ended up terrified anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It did.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm understanding you. You've been living with serious pain for years, and the medications haven't been enough on their own — so you found something that helped, the wine. You've been carrying all of that quietly, trying not to worry anyone. But last week, something went wrong that you can't fully account for. And I'm hearing that, for the first time, part of you is wondering whether this has gotten a little bit out of your control.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... I don't know. Maybe. I thought I had it under control. I've always handled things myself. I raised three kids on my own, you know. I don't — I've never been someone who asks for help.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Someone who has carried that much for that long — what would it mean to you, to actually let someone help you with this one?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I never really thought about it that way. Maybe it wouldn't be... I mean, if I could feel better — actually feel better — and my daughter wasn't afraid every time the phone rings... that would be something. That would be worth it, I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see a version of this where the pain is managed and your daughter isn't afraid to answer the phone. That matters to you deeply.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. It really does. I'm not saying I know how to get there. But I'm willing to... I don't know, maybe talk about it more. See what you have to say. I haven't got anything to lose at this point, have I.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. You mentioned when you booked this that things got rocky — I want to hear about it. What's been going on since we last talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't know. It's been a week, man. My advisor called me in again and I just... I'm so tired of being called in about stuff. Like, I'm showing up, aren't I? I'm doing what I'm supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're putting in the effort, and it still feels like you're being called on the carpet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, yeah I drink after shifts, so what? Every bartender I know does. That's just — that's just the job. You stand on your feet for eight hours, you deal with people all night, you need something to come down. That's not a problem, that's just how it works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That whole culture is real — the way the industry runs, everyone around you handles it the same way. I'm curious though, what did your advisor actually say that got under your skin this time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said I looked — and I quote — 'not okay.' And that I'd been missing morning classes. Which, like... okay, fair, I have been.
