But I'm working until 2, 3 AM and then I wind down with a few drinks, and then I'm supposed to be up at 8? That's not a drinking problem, that's a scheduling problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot — late nights, school, trying to decompress enough to actually sleep. And you're still showing up. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I mean... I'm trying. But lately the 'few drinks to wind down' has kind of become more than a few. And I woke up this morning and realized I literally cannot think of the last time I went to bed sober. Like, I actually tried to remember and I couldn't. And that... that kind of freaked me out, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment this morning — when you tried to remember and couldn't. What was that like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Bad weird. Like... I'm 27. I'm not supposed to be — I don't know. My dad had a really bad drinking thing and I always told myself I was different. That I had it under control. And sitting there this morning I was like, do I? Do I actually have it under control?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been holding onto that — the belief that you're different from your dad. And this morning something cracked that open a little.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, I still think I'm different. I'm not — it's not like that. But I guess I've been saying that for a while without actually, like, checking. Actually stopping and checking in with myself. And maybe I should've been doing that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real honesty to sit with that question instead of just pushing it away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I would've even gone there if she hadn't called me in. Maybe I needed someone to... say something out loud. Which is a weird thing to admit. ... I don't love that that's true.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together. You've been working late nights, drinking to wind down, and that's turned into every single night with no break. This morning you had a moment where you couldn't account for a sober night, and it scared you — partly because of what you've seen in your family. And underneath all the frustration with your advisor, there's a part of you that's actually glad someone said something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — I hate that that's accurate, but it is. I don't want to be the guy who needed someone else to see it before he did. But I guess that's kind of what happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned actually checking in with yourself — what would that look like for you going forward? What would be a real first step?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... not drinking every single night. Even one night where I do something else. Go for a run, watch something, I don't know. I haven't done that in a really long time. Like, I can't even remember what I used to do instead. But that feels like it could be a start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One night where you choose something different. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, I guess it isn't. ... I think I actually want to try it. Which is — that's kind of new for me, honestly. Usually I come in here ready to argue my way out of this whole conversation.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — welcome, I guess is the word. I know coming here wasn't exactly your idea, so I appreciate you showing up anyway. What would make today actually worth your time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My wife basically said it's this or... yeah. So here I am. I don't really think talking to a stranger is gonna fix anything, but, you know. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the stakes got high enough that you figured — alright, one more shot. And part of you already came in pretty sure it won't work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I've done this before. Therapy. It felt like a lot of talking about feelings and nothing actually changing. I'm not trying to be a jerk, I just — I don't see what's different this time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That actually makes a lot of sense. You came in, did the work, it didn't stick — and now someone's sent you back for round two. I'd be skeptical too, honestly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right? Like, am I the problem? Is that what we're doing here? Because it feels like every time I end up in a chair like this it's because I'm the problem and everyone else is just... look. I drink. I know I drink. I don't need a worksheet to tell me that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know. No convincing needed — you've clocked it yourself. That actually puts you ahead of most people who sit in that chair. No worksheets, I promise.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Huh. Yeah. I mean — I'm not an idiot. I know what I'm doing. I just — it's not like I wake up wanting to feel like garbage. It started as... I don't know. It helped. For a while it actually helped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Helped with what?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The... the depression stuff, I guess. Like when everything just gets too heavy and you can't — I can't think straight, can't sleep, can't do anything. A few drinks and I could actually function. That sounds insane, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound insane at all. It sounds like you found something that worked — until it stopped working, or started costing more than it gave back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's kind of exactly it. At some point I couldn't even tell anymore — am I drinking because of the depression, or is the drinking making the depression worse? It's like... I don't know. Chicken and egg.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've got two things feeding each other — the depression pushing you toward the drinking, the drinking maybe making the depression heavier — and you're stuck in the middle of it trying to hold everything together. And somehow in all of that, you still got yourself here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it out loud like that it sounds... exhausting. And yeah, I guess it is. I'm tired. I'm genuinely just — I'm tired of all of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you — not to your wife, not to anyone else — what would it actually mean to you if things were different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I used to be different. Like I used to actually enjoy things. I coached my nephew's little league team. Haven't done that in like two years. My brother stopped asking. I think about that sometimes, more than I probably should.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The guy who coached little league — you miss him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, I do. I didn't really think about it like that but... yeah. My wife — she married that guy, you know? Not whatever I've turned into. I don't even blame her for being fed up. I'm fed up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you walked in here today pretty sure this was a waste of time — and somewhere in the last half hour you've told me you're exhausted, that you miss who you used to be, and that part of you actually gives a damn about finding your way back there. That's not nothing. What feels like one thing — just one — you might actually be willing to look at?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... maybe the depression stuff. Like actually dealing with that instead of just — you know. If I wasn't waking up feeling like a brick wall every morning, maybe I wouldn't need the other thing as much. I don't know. Maybe.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back. A lot of people don't make it to a second session, and you did. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I almost didn't, honestly. I sat in the parking lot for about fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes in the parking lot, and you still walked in. What was going through your mind while you were sitting out there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I kept thinking, what's the point, really. But then I... the doctor's office called again this week about those lab numbers and I just — I couldn't keep ignoring it. I don't even want to think about what they mean.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The call felt like something pressing in on you. Hard to push away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They want me to come in and I... I already know what they're going to say. The liver enzymes or whatever. I've read enough online to know what that usually means. And I'm just — I'm not ready to sit in that office and be lectured at. I'm 55, not a teenager.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already have a sense of what the results might be pointing to. What does it bring up for you, sitting with that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Fear, I suppose. But also... I don't know, it's like, even if I know it's bad, I can't just stop. I'm not drinking because I want to get drunk. I'm not some... I'm not that kind of person. It's just the evenings. After dinner when the house is — it's so quiet. Harold and I, we'd sit after dinner and watch TV. Stupid stuff. Whatever was on. And now it's just me and that quiet and the wine makes it... softer somehow.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking has been filling something that Harold used to fill.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yes. I mean — it sounds terrible when you say it like that. My daughter Sarah keeps calling and I don't pick up because she'll hear it in my voice. I don't want her worrying. She's got her own kids, her own life. I've just been... managing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're trying to protect Sarah from carrying something extra, while you carry all of it alone. That's not weakness — that's actually someone who thinks about the people she loves even when she's hurting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I never — hm. I always figured I was just being a coward. Hiding from her. *pause* I haven't really let anyone in since Harold died. Not really.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you think about where things are headed — the lab results, the evenings, pulling away from Sarah — what does your gut tell you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My gut tells me I'm in trouble. *quietly* Some nights it's most of a bottle. I know that's... I know. And I'm tired all the time. I don't sleep well. I wake up at three in the morning and just lie there. Harold would be so upset with me right now. He always said I was stronger than I gave myself credit for. Thirty-one years we were together and he never once gave up on me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you can still hear Harold's voice. And it's saying something different than what you've been doing these past eight months.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... *long pause* ... Yeah. He'd be sitting right here telling me to get my act together. Not meanly. He wasn't like that. He'd just — he'd hold my hand and say, Donna, you're still here. You've got to live. *voice cracks* I miss him so much it's like something physical. Like a hole. And I know the drinking isn't fixing that. I know it. I just... I didn't know what else to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think you've said something really important today. You lost Harold eight months ago, and the evenings are the hardest — the quiet is unbearable, and the wine has been the one thing that softens it. You've been protecting Sarah by staying at a distance, carrying the grief alone. Your body is now telling you something has to change. And underneath all of it, there's Harold's voice — and your own — saying you're still here and you're stronger than this feels. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: *quietly* Yeah. That's... *exhales* ...that's exactly it. I think I've just needed someone to say it out loud. I couldn't say it to myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you just said — what feels like one thing, even something small, that you might want to do differently this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'm going to call Sarah back. I don't have to tell her everything. But I've been so alone and I — *pause* — I'm going to go to the doctor's appointment too. I keep canceling it. I'm going to actually go. Harold would want me to go.
